anchor: The central question is: > When do two pieces of evidence constitute the same evidential contribution, when are they dependent transformations, and when are they genuinely independent observations?
statement: Frames the file's governing problem: distinguishing same-contribution, dependent-transformation, and genuinely-independent evidence, calling it more fundamental than choosing an aggregation formula because getting it wrong makes 'every downstream confidence, conflict, gap, and conclusion' wrong.

anchor: Identity ... e_1=e_2 ... This is a data/infrastructure property. ... Equivalence ... e_1\sim e_2 ... Independence ... e_1\perp e_2 ... Equivalence\neq\text{Independence}
statement: Defines three formally distinct evidence relations: Identity (e1=e2, literally the same record — same hash/document/observation ID, a data/infrastructure property), Equivalence (e1~e2, different records expressing the same underlying proposition, illustrated with two differently-worded documents both asserting Nexus 3.69), and Independence (e1⊥e2, genuinely separate information, illustrated by an API report and an independent filesystem inspection both reporting 3.69); concludes Equivalence ≠ Independence.

anchor: Dependency is actually richer than equivalence ... Database → LLM → Architecture report → Human summary ... e_1\rightarrow e_2\rightarrow e_3\rightarrow e_4 ... Dependency\neq\text{Equivalence}
statement: Shows via a Database→LLM→Architecture-report→Human-summary chain that later items can causally/epistemically depend on earlier ones (e1→e2→e3→e4) while having different semantic content (e.g. 'Nexus=3.69' vs 'Nexus is running an older version'), so Dependency ≠ Equivalence.

anchor: We therefore need an Evidence Graph ... G_E=(V,E) ... V=\text{Evidence Objects} ... This graph is not merely metadata. It affects the mathematics of evidence aggregation.
statement: Introduces an Evidence Graph G_E=(V,E) whose vertices are Evidence Objects and whose edges represent provenance/dependency (e.g. Nexus API observation --DERIVED_FROM--> LLM output --INTERPRETED_AS--> Assertion --REVIEWED_BY--> Human review), asserting the graph is not mere metadata but affects the mathematics of evidence aggregation.

anchor: Define the underlying observation ... UnderlyingObservation(e)=o ... means that these are multiple representations of one underlying observation. This is much more precise than simply saying "duplicate."
statement: Defines a function UnderlyingObservation(e)=o mapping an evidence record (database entry, screenshot, LLM extraction, human report) to the single underlying observation event it represents, offered as a more precise substitute for calling records 'duplicates'.

anchor: Evidence provenance becomes causal structure ... e_j\prec e_i ... Dependency\Rightarrow NonIndependent ... NonIndependent \not\Rightarrow DirectDependency ... Two sources can share a common ancestor without one directly producing the other.
statement: Defines e_j≺e_i ('e_i was produced using e_j') and states the conservative rule Dependency⇒NonIndependent, while noting the converse fails: NonIndependent does not imply DirectDependency, because two sources can share a common ancestor without one producing the other directly.

anchor: Common-source dependency ... Original document / LLM A, LLM B ... LLM_A\not\rightarrow LLM_B ... CommonAncestor(LLM_A,LLM_B) ... CommonSource(e_i,e_j) as a first-class relationship. This protects us against **correlated evidence inflation**.
statement: Introduces CommonSource(e_i,e_j) as a first-class relationship for cases where two evidence items (e.g. LLM A and LLM B outputs) neither directly depend on each other but share a common ancestor document, warning that treating such items as independent corroboration causes correlated evidence inflation.

anchor: Three epistemic dependency classes ... Class 1 — Same contribution ... e_i\equiv e_j ... Count once. ... Class 2 — Dependent contribution ... e_i\leadsto e_j ... Do not treat them as independent corroboration. ... Class 3 — Independent contribution ... e_i\perp e_j ... They may contribute independen
statement: Defines a three-class taxonomy for evidence-pair handling: Class 1 Same contribution (e_i≡e_j, count once), Class 2 Dependent contribution (e_i⤳e_j, never treat as independent corroboration), Class 3 Independent contribution (e_i⊥e_j, may contribute independently, explicitly qualified as 'under the selected policy').

anchor: UnknownDependency\neq\nIndependence ... UnknownDependency\Rightarrow Do\ not\ assume\ independent\ corroboration. This is a very strong candidate for a kernel invariant.
statement: States the rule UnknownDependency ≠ Independence and, conservatively, UnknownDependency ⇒ do not assume independent corroboration, explicitly flagging this as 'a very strong candidate for a kernel invariant' for KnowledgeOS.

assumptions.statement: Conservative epistemic reasoning treats unknown dependency as non-independence by default.

anchor: We should not say: > "Unknown dependency means the evidence is useless." That would be too strong. ... UnknownIndependence\neq NoEvidence
statement: Corrects an over-strong reading of the unknown-dependency rule: unknown dependency does not mean the evidence is useless — it means its incremental independent evidential contribution cannot be safely quantified, while the evidence may still be relevant, historically useful, supportive, contradictory, or useful for discovery; formalized as UnknownIndependence ≠ NoEvidence.

anchor: The Evidence Identity relation ... e_i\sim_E e_j ... Reflexivity ... Symmetry ... Transitivity ... \sim_E\text{ should be an equivalence relation} ... according to an explicitly declared equivalence policy ... because semantic equivalence is not always decidable automatically.
statement: Defines an Evidence Identity relation e_i~_E e_j meant to satisfy reflexivity, symmetry and transitivity (a genuine equivalence relation), but qualifies this against an 'explicitly declared equivalence policy' since semantic equivalence is not always automatically decidable.

assumptions.statement: ~_E is only well-defined relative to an explicitly declared equivalence policy.
assumptions.anchor: according to an explicitly declared equivalence policy

anchor: This is where LLMs become useful—but dangerous ... LLM: CandidateEquivalence(e1,e2) ... KnowledgeOS: EquivalenceStatus = Proposed ... Rule / human / deterministic check: Confirmed ... LLM\ judgment \neq authoritative epistemic fact
statement: Constrains the role of LLMs in establishing evidence equivalence: an LLM may propose CandidateEquivalence(e1,e2), which KnowledgeOS records as EquivalenceStatus=Proposed, but only a rule, human, or deterministic check can confirm it — 'LLM judgment ≠ authoritative epistemic fact'.

anchor: DDD model ... Evidence ... Provenance ... EvidenceIdentity ... DependencyAssessment ... EvidenceAssessment ... Notice that **EvidenceAssessment does not contain Truth**.
statement: Sketches a DDD model with five entities — Evidence (EvidenceId, Proposition, Polarity, Source, AcquiredAt, Context, Quality), Provenance (parent/relation/transformation/actor/timestamp), EvidenceIdentity (UnderlyingObservationId, EquivalenceClass, IdentityConfidence), DependencyAssessment (EvidenceA/B, Relationship, Status, Basis), and EvidenceAssessment (PositiveSupport, NegativeSupport, Uncertainty, DependencyStructure, Quality, Qualifications) — and explicitly notes EvidenceAssessment does not contain Truth.

anchor: Mathematical structure emerging ... \mathcal E \rightarrow \mathcal E/\sim_E \rightarrow D \rightarrow Q \rightarrow \oplus_\rho \rightarrow EA ... This is becoming a genuine computational calculus.
statement: Assembles the pipeline: raw evidence set E, quotient by equivalence E/~_E, dependency function D:(E/~_E)^2→{Dependent,Independent,Unknown}, quality function Q:E/~_E→Q, policy-specific aggregation ⊕_ρ, producing an EvidenceAssessment EA — described as 'becoming a genuine computational calculus'.

anchor: One thing we must NOT do ... Independent(e_i,e_j) = SemanticDifference(e_i,e_j) ... Sensor A: temperature = 20°C Sensor B: temperature = 20°C ... Same proposition. Different observations. ... SemanticEquivalence\neq EvidentialIndependence. This distinction is fundamental.
statement: Warns against the mathematically wrong definition Independent(e_i,e_j)=SemanticDifference(e_i,e_j), using two sensors reporting the identical 20°C reading as independent observations of the same proposition to establish SemanticEquivalence ≠ EvidentialIndependence as a fundamental distinction.

anchor: Our new test cases ... Case A — Exact duplicate ... Case B — Semantic duplicate ... Case C — Independent identical observations ... Case D — LLM transformation ... Case E — Common-source outputs ... Case F — Unknown provenance
statement: Lays out six test cases with expected contribution counts: (A) exact duplicate e1=e2 → 1 contribution; (B) semantic duplicate e1~_E e2 → 1 contribution; (C) independent identical observations e1~_P e2 but e1⊥e2 → 2 contributions; (D) LLM transformation e1→LLM(e1) → 1 independent contribution; (E) common-source outputs e0→e1, e0→e2 → not independent; (F) unknown provenance → do not assume independence.

anchor: A provisional theorem ... Evidence multiplicity is not equivalent to evidential independence. ... |E| \neq |\text{IndependentContributions}(E)| ... InformationVolume\neq EvidenceStrength ... Ten documents copied from one source do not necessarily provide ten pieces of evidence.
statement: States a provisional theorem that evidence multiplicity is not equivalent to evidential independence, formalized as |E| ≠ |IndependentContributions(E)| and InformationVolume ≠ EvidenceStrength, illustrated by ten documents copied from one source not necessarily providing ten pieces of evidence; called 'a very important KnowledgeOS principle'.

anchor: Where we are now ... Strongly established: Evidence Identity, Evidence Equivalence, Evidence Dependency, Common-Source Detection, Unknown Dependency ... Still open ... How can KnowledgeOS computationally determine independence? ... Absolute epistemic independence is generally not computable from arb
statement: Summarizes five 'strongly established' concepts (Evidence Identity, Equivalence, Dependency, Common-Source Detection, Unknown Dependency) and states the remaining open question — how KnowledgeOS can computationally determine independence — with the explicit limitation that absolute epistemic independence is generally not computable from arbitrary documents alone, framed as 'a boundary condition of the problem' rather than a KnowledgeOS failure.

anchor: the next step should be to define an **Operational Independence Test**: Independence_\rho(e_i,e_j,G_E,C) \rightarrow \{Confirmed,Rejected,Unknown\} ... test whether that operation is actually implementable from our available inputs: documents, databases, Internet sources, rules, manifests, human ins
statement: Proposes the next step: define an Operational Independence Test Independence_ρ(e_i,e_j,G_E,C)→{Confirmed,Rejected,Unknown} and test its implementability against KnowledgeOS's actual available inputs (documents, databases, Internet sources, rules, manifests, human instructions, scope, constitution, settings, ADRs, textbooks, AI/LLM outputs) as 'the next computational-closure test' — directly taken up by the immediately following file.

lineage_claims.quote: That is the next computational-closure test.

anchor: Can KnowledgeOS determine whether two evidence items are independent using computable information? ... True Independence ... Operationally Established Independence ... KnowledgeOS cannot generally prove metaphysical independence. It can determine independence relative to an explicit evidence model.
statement: Distinguishes True (metaphysical) Independence, which KnowledgeOS cannot generally prove, from Operationally Established Independence, which it can determine relative to an explicit evidence model; defines Ind_ρ(e_i,e_j,G,C)→{Independent,Dependent,Unknown} over evidence pair, provenance graph G, context C, and independence policy ρ.

type_signature.domain: Evidence x Evidence x Graph x Context

anchor: What information can KnowledgeOS actually inspect? ... M(e)=(Source,AcquisitionEvent,Timestamp,Actor,Method,ParentEvidence,Transformation,Location,Content,Context)
statement: Defines the inspectable evidence-metadata tuple M(e)=(Source, AcquisitionEvent, Timestamp, Actor, Method, ParentEvidence, Transformation, Location, Content, Context), illustrated by contrasting a direct Nexus-API observation with an LLM summarization whose Parent is that observation.

anchor: The first deterministic rule ... If e_i\leadsto e_j in the provenance graph, then Ind(e_i,e_j)=Dependent. This is deterministic. No LLM is required.
statement: States a deterministic rule requiring no LLM: if e_i leads to e_j in the provenance graph (e.g. Database → LLM extraction), then Ind(e_i,e_j)=Dependent.

anchor: Common ancestry ... CommonAncestor(A,B)=D ... we cannot safely say A\perp B ... CommonAncestor(e_i,e_j) \Rightarrow Independent(e_i,e_j)\neq Confirmed ... The result should normally be Unknown unless the policy provides a justified way to establish conditional independence.
statement: For two evidence items with no direct edge but a common ancestor (e.g. two LLMs, A and B, both reading Document D), states CommonAncestor(e_i,e_j) ⇒ Independent(e_i,e_j)≠Confirmed, with the default result Unknown unless the policy justifies conditional independence.

anchor: Different sources do not automatically mean independent ... Reuters → Document A, Reuters → Document B ... Source(A)\neq Source(B) does not prove A\perp B ... DifferentSource\not\Rightarrow Independent
statement: Warns that different apparent sources (e.g. two documents both ultimately from Reuters) do not prove independence, since both may originate from the same underlying report: DifferentSource ⇏ Independent.

anchor: Different acquisition events are stronger ... Sensor A → 20°C at 10:00, Sensor B → 20°C at 10:00 ... independent sensors; independent acquisition mechanisms; independent provenance; no shared upstream observation. Then we can establish OperationallyIndependent(e_1,e_2) under the declared policy. Not
statement: Shows that independent acquisition mechanisms/provenance (e.g. two separate sensors reporting the same 20°C reading with no shared upstream observation) can establish OperationallyIndependent(e1,e2) under a declared policy, stressing the qualifier 'operationally'.

anchor: We therefore need an independence evidence vector ... I(e_i,e_j)=(i_S,i_A,i_P,i_M,i_T,i_C) ... Source independence ... Acquisition independence ... Provenance independence ... Method independence ... Temporal independence ... Common-ancestor status ... Each can be {Confirmed,Rejected,Unknown}. This
statement: Proposes representing independence not as a single boolean but as a six-dimension vector I(e_i,e_j)=(i_S,i_A,i_P,i_M,i_T,i_C) — Source, Acquisition, Provenance, Method, Temporal independence and Common-ancestor status — each valued {Confirmed,Rejected,Unknown}, to preserve uncertainty.

anchor: Why not simply calculate an independence score? We should resist IndependenceScore=0.87 because that number would obscure why the evidence is considered independent. ... This is much more auditable.
statement: Argues against collapsing independence into a single score like IndependenceScore=0.87, since a scalar obscures why evidence is considered independent, in favor of an itemized per-dimension Confirmed/Rejected breakdown that is auditable.

anchor: Formal decision rule ... Ind_\rho(e_i,e_j,G,C) = Dependent if dependency is established; Independent if all required independence conditions hold; Unknown otherwise. The important word is required ... because the conditions depend on policy. For a high-risk security decision, we may require very str
statement: Gives the formal decision rule for Ind_ρ as a three-way case split (Dependent/Independent/Unknown) keyed on policy-defined 'required' conditions, noting the required strength of independence is itself policy-dependent (e.g. stronger for high-risk security decisions than exploratory research).

anchor: The three-valued result is important ... I=\{I,D,U\} ... better than {True,False} because Unknown\neq False and Unknown\neq True. ... Absence of evidence for independence is not evidence of dependence, but neither is it evidence of independence.
statement: Argues the three-valued result set {Independent, Dependent, Unknown} is necessary rather than a boolean, since Unknown≠False and Unknown≠True, stating the central KnowledgeOS principle: 'Absence of evidence for independence is not evidence of dependence, but neither is it evidence of independence.'

anchor: DDD representation ... IndependenceAssessment ... EvidenceA, EvidenceB, SourceRelation, AcquisitionRelation, ProvenanceRelation, MethodRelation, CommonAncestor, Result, Policy, Basis, Timestamp ... The result is a domain object, not merely a database flag.
statement: Models the independence determination as an IndependenceAssessment domain object (EvidenceA/B, per-dimension relation fields, CommonAncestor, Result, Policy, Basis, Timestamp) rather than a bare database flag.

anchor: Domain invariant ... Dependent(e_i,e_j) \Rightarrow \neg Independent(e_i,e_j) ... Unknown(e_i,e_j) \Rightarrow \neg ConfirmedIndependent(e_i,e_j). The second is particularly important.
statement: States two formal invariants: Dependent(e_i,e_j) ⇒ ¬Independent(e_i,e_j), and Unknown(e_i,e_j) ⇒ ¬ConfirmedIndependent(e_i,e_j), flagging the second as particularly important.

anchor: Test cases ... Case A — Exact duplicate ... Dependent/SameContribution ... Case B — LLM transformation ... Dependent ... Case C — Two LLMs reading the same document ... Unknown ... Case D — Two independent sensors ... Independent ... Case E — Two websites copying the same source ... Dependent/Correl
statement: Works six test cases through Ind_ρ: (A) exact duplicate → Dependent/SameContribution; (B) e2=LLM(e1) → Dependent; (C) two LLMs reading the same document D → Unknown (absent a conditional-independence policy); (D) two independent sensors → Independent under policy; (E) two websites copying one source → Dependent/Correlated; (F) missing provenance → Unknown.

anchor: This gives us an important KnowledgeOS law ... Independence must be established, not assumed. ... Independence(e_i,e_j)=Confirmed only when the declared policy's conditions are satisfied. Otherwise Unknown.
statement: Provisionally adopts the KnowledgeOS law 'Independence must be established, not assumed', formalized as Independence(e_i,e_j)=Confirmed only when the declared policy's conditions are satisfied, else Unknown.

anchor: One subtle statistical correction ... Operational independence is not necessarily statistical independence. ... both may be affected by the same environmental bias. OperationallyIndependent \not\Rightarrow StatisticallyIndependent ... OperationalIndependence \rightarrow Evidence about possible stati
statement: Introduces a key caveat: OperationallyIndependent does not imply StatisticallyIndependent (e.g. two sensors with separate acquisition/hardware may still share an environmental bias); operational independence only provides evidence about possible statistical independence, and a Bayesian factorization P(E1,E2|H)=P(E1|H)P(E2|H) needs its own justified assumptions — hence Evidence Architecture and Statistical Inference Policy must be kept separate.

anchor: Step 1 conclusion ... operational independence is computable in a qualified sense. ... it must not claim universal statistical independence merely from metadata.
statement: Concludes Step 1: KnowledgeOS can deterministically inspect provenance, dependency, common ancestry, acquisition events, sources, methods, and context to produce Independent/Dependent/Unknown under a declared policy, but must never claim universal statistical independence from metadata alone.

anchor: Step 2 ... How does KnowledgeOS determine whether two evidence items are the same underlying evidential contribution, merely semantically equivalent, or genuinely distinct observations? That takes us into the Evidence Identity / Equivalence Calculus ... I suggest we tackle that next—and test it with
statement: Closes by posing Step 2's question — same underlying evidential contribution vs semantic equivalence vs genuinely distinct observation — as the Evidence Identity/Equivalence Calculus, to be tackled next via concrete examples rather than abstract definition; taken up by the immediately following file.

lineage_claims.quote: I suggest we tackle that next

anchor:
two statements can look identical while representing different observations, or look different while representing the same underlying observation. ... Identity 
eq Semantic Equivalence 
eq Same Observation 
eq Independence
statement: States that KnowledgeOS must keep four concepts separate — Identity, Semantic Equivalence, Same Observation, and Independence — warning that statements can look identical while representing different observations, or look different while representing the same underlying observation.

anchor: Evidence identity ... e_1=e_2 means they are literally the same Evidence object ... ID(e)=Hash(canonical(e)) ... Hash(e_1)=Hash(e_2) \Rightarrow same canonical representation but it does not establish that two independently acquired observations are the same real-world event.
statement: Defines Evidence Identity e1=e2 (literally the same object, e.g. an accidentally double-imported database record) via ID(e)=Hash(canonical(e)) or a stable acquisition identifier, but notes hash equality establishes same canonical representation only — not that two independently acquired observations are the same real-world event.

anchor: Semantic equivalence ... e_1\approx_P e_2 if they express the same proposition under a specified semantic interpretation. This is propositional equivalence, not evidential identity.
statement: Defines propositional/semantic equivalence e1≈_P e2 (e.g. 'Nexus version is 3.69' vs 'The installed Nexus instance runs release 3.69'), explicitly distinct from evidential identity.

anchor: Same underlying observation ... Underlying(e_1)=Underlying(e_2)=o ... Therefore they should not count as two independent observations.
statement: Defines same-underlying-observation via Underlying(e1)=Underlying(e2)=o (e.g. a database record and a PDF generated from it), concluding such pairs should not count as two independent observations.

anchor: Independently acquired identical observations ... e_1\approx_Pe_2 ... Underlying(e_1)\neq Underlying(e_2) ... e_1\perp e_2 ... This is the case that a simple deduplication algorithm would destroy. ... Semantic equivalence must NOT imply deduplication. That is a critical invariant.
statement: Using a Nexus API report and an independent filesystem inspection both asserting the same proposition, shows they can be semantically equivalent yet have different underlying observations and be operationally independent — naming the critical invariant that semantic equivalence must NOT imply deduplication, since a naive deduplicator would destroy this corroborating evidence.

anchor: Four relations ... Identity: e_1 =_I e_2 ... Semantic equivalence: e_1 =_P e_2 ... Observation equivalence: e_1 =_O e_2 ... Dependency: e_1\prec e_2 ... e_1\perp_\rho e_2 Operationally independent under policy \rho.
statement: Formally names four relations: Identity (=_I, same evidence object), Semantic equivalence (=_P, same proposition), Observation equivalence (=_O, same underlying observation/event), Dependency (≺, e2 produced using e1), plus operational independence under policy ρ (⊥_ρ).

anchor: Case A — Exact duplicate ... e_1=_I e_2 ... one evidential contribution ... Case B — Same observation, different representation ... e_1\neq_I e_2 but e_1=_Oe_2 and e_2\prec e_1 ... one underlying observation ... Case C — LLM transformation ... e_1\approx_Pe_2 and e_1\prec e_2 ... e_2 is not independ
statement: Works Cases A-C: (A) exact duplicate API record → e1=_I e2 → one evidential contribution; (B) raw API response vs extracted JSON field → not identical but same observation and derived → one underlying observation; (C) API says 3.69 vs LLM paraphrase → propositionally equivalent and derived (e1≺e2) → the LLM output is not independent evidence, only a derived representation.

anchor: Case D — Two LLMs reading the same document ... D\prec e_1, D\prec e_2 ... e_1\not\perp e_2 at least not automatically. The correct status is CommonSource and therefore usually Independence=Unknown under our conservative policy.
statement: Case D: two LLMs (A, B) both reading Document D produce e1, e2 that are derived from a common source and not automatically independent; the correct status is CommonSource, and Independence should default to Unknown under the conservative policy.

anchor: Case E — Two independent measurements ... e_1\approx_Pe_2 but e_1\neq_Oe_2 and possibly e_1\perp_\rho e_2. Therefore both can contribute. ... Same proposition + different independent observation = corroboration.
statement: Case E: API and filesystem both reporting 3.69 are propositionally equivalent but not the same observation and may be operationally independent, so both can contribute — formalized as 'Same proposition + different independent observation = corroboration'.

anchor: Case F — Same source, different times ... e_1\approx_Pe_2 they represent two acquisition events. So Same proposition\neq same observation.
statement: Case F: the same value (3.69) reported at two different times (09:00 and 15:00) is propositionally equivalent but not the same observation, since the acquisition events differ — Same proposition ≠ same observation.

anchor: Case G — Different values, same observation ... "Nexus 3.69" ... LLM incorrectly extracts ... "Nexus 3.70" ... D\prec e_1, D\prec e_2 but e_1\not\approx_Pe_2. So we have Contradictory derived assertions, not contradictory independent observations. ... Conflict type: DERIVATION_CONFLICT ... Underlyin
statement: Case G: a document stating 'Nexus 3.69' and an LLM's incorrect extraction 'Nexus 3.70' both derive from the same document but disagree propositionally — classified as a DERIVATION_CONFLICT (1 independent observation, 2 derived interpretations) rather than a contradiction between independent observations, judged far more informative than 'two sources disagree'.

anchor: This leads to an evidence lineage graph ... G_E=(V,L) ... L=\{DerivedFrom,ExtractedFrom,TransformedFrom,SummarizedFrom,CopiedFrom,ObservedFrom,ReviewedFrom\} ... KnowledgeOS can trace e\rightarrow parents(e) all the way to the original observation.
statement: Proposes an explicit evidence lineage graph G_E=(V,L) with a typed edge-label set L={DerivedFrom, ExtractedFrom, TransformedFrom, SummarizedFrom, CopiedFrom, ObservedFrom, ReviewedFrom}, letting KnowledgeOS trace any evidence object to its parents up to the original observation.

anchor: We can define the evidence root ... Root(e) as the set of upstream acquisition events from which the evidence ultimately derives. ... Root(e_1)=Root(e_2) should not automatically be treated as independent.
statement: Defines Root(e) as the set of upstream acquisition events an evidence object ultimately derives from (illustrated by Database observation→JSON extraction→LLM interpretation→Architecture report all sharing Root={o1}); evidence objects sharing a Root should not automatically be treated as independent.

anchor: But there is a problem ... Sensor A observation, Sensor B observation ↓ Common weather event. Both have a common real-world cause. Yet they may still be useful independent measurements. Therefore CommonCause\neq SameObservation and CommonCause\neq AutomaticDependence. This takes us into statistical
statement: Qualifies the Root/CommonSource machinery: two sensors sharing a common real-world cause (a weather event) can still be useful independent measurements, so CommonCause ≠ SameObservation and CommonCause ≠ AutomaticDependence — statistical dependence must remain a separate, policy/model-dependent question.

anchor: The resulting classification ... Relationship(e_i,e_j) ... IDENTICAL, SAME_OBSERVATION, DERIVED, SEMANTICALLY_EQUIVALENT, COMMON_SOURCE, INDEPENDENT, CONTRADICTORY, UNKNOWN. But these should not be a single enum. That would again collapse different dimensions. Instead, they are relations that can co
statement: Warns against collapsing evidence relationships into a single enum (IDENTICAL/SAME_OBSERVATION/DERIVED/SEMANTICALLY_EQUIVALENT/COMMON_SOURCE/INDEPENDENT/CONTRADICTORY/UNKNOWN), proposing instead independent coexisting boolean relations per evidence pair for expressiveness.

anchor: The mathematical structure ... G_E=(V,L_1,L_2,\ldots,L_n) ... L_I=Identity, L_P=PropositionalEquivalence, L_O=ObservationIdentity, L_D=Dependency, L_C=CommonSource, L_X=Contradiction. This is much more mathematically appropriate than one "evidence similarity score."
statement: Formalizes the evidence structure as a multi-relational graph G_E=(V,L1,...,Ln) with named relation layers (Identity, PropositionalEquivalence, ObservationIdentity, Dependency, CommonSource, Contradiction), argued to be more mathematically appropriate than a single evidence-similarity score.

anchor: DDD consequence ... EvidenceLineage ... Where did this evidence come from? ... EvidenceRelation ... How does this evidence relate to another evidence object? ... EvidenceEquivalence ... Do these represent the same proposition or observation? These should not be merged into Evidence.
statement: Introduces three distinct DDD concepts that must not be merged into a single Evidence entity: EvidenceLineage (provenance), EvidenceRelation (inter-evidence relationships), and EvidenceEquivalence (propositional/observational sameness).

anchor: Critical invariant ... SemanticEquivalent(e_1,e_2) \not\Rightarrow SameObservation(e_1,e_2) ... SameObservation(e_1,e_2) \Rightarrow NonIndependent(e_1,e_2) ... while SemanticEquivalent(e_1,e_2) \land Independent(e_1,e_2) is perfectly valid. That last case is corroboration.
statement: States the invariants SemanticEquivalent ⇏ SameObservation and SameObservation ⇒ NonIndependent, while SemanticEquivalent ∧ Independent is valid and constitutes corroboration.

anchor: What can be deterministic? ... Deterministically computable: exact identity; cryptographic hash equality; explicit provenance ... Algorithmically inferable: semantic equivalence; copied content; common source ... Not universally decidable: metaphysical sameness of observations; absolute independence
statement: Classifies evidence-relation determinations into three computability tiers — deterministically computable (hash equality, explicit provenance/parent-child, timestamps, source IDs), algorithmically inferable (semantic equivalence, copied content, common source, likely contradiction), and not universally decidable (metaphysical sameness, absolute independence, truth) — requiring every inferred relation to carry a status of Confirmed | Inferred | Proposed | Unknown.

anchor: This is a major architectural principle ... Fact about provenance ... from ... Inference about provenance ... Fact: LLM input = Document D ... Inference: LLM output semantically represents proposition P ... KnowledgeOS should never silently promote the second into the first.
statement: States the architectural principle that Fact-about-provenance (e.g. LLM input = Document D) must be kept distinct from Inference-about-provenance (e.g. LLM output semantically represents proposition P), and KnowledgeOS must never silently promote an inference into a fact.

anchor: We have therefore completed Step 2 conceptually ... Evidence + Lineage + Relations + Equivalence + Dependency + Assessment rather than Evidence+Score. This is a substantial improvement.
statement: Summarizes Step 2's conclusion: the Evidence model is now Evidence + Lineage + Relations + Equivalence + Dependency + Assessment, replacing a naive Evidence+Score model.

anchor: Step 3 — The next problem ... Given a set of evidence objects and their relationships, how does KnowledgeOS construct an Evidence Assessment without double-counting, losing contradictions, or inventing certainty? ... \mathcal E,G_E,P,C,\rho \rightarrow EA ... The next step will be to construct the E
statement: Poses Step 3's problem — constructing an Evidence Assessment EA from (evidence set, lineage graph, propositions, context, policy) without double-counting, losing contradictions, or inventing certainty — announcing the next file will build an Evidence Assessment Algebra from these relations rather than choosing an aggregation formula first.

lineage_claims.quote: The next step will be to construct the Evidence Assessment Algebra

anchor: we should not invent a universal formula for "evidence strength." ... What is an Evidence Assessment? ... An Evidence Assessment is a structured, policy-governed evaluation of the evidential support, opposition, uncertainty, provenance, and applicability of a proposition within a specified context.
statement: Defines Evidence Assessment EA=(S+,S-,U,Q,V,D,X,Π) — Supporting evidence, Opposing evidence, Uncertainty, Quality, Validity/temporal, Dependency structure, Context/applicability, Provenance — as a structured, policy-governed evaluation that explicitly excludes Truth: EA evaluates evidence, it does not establish reality.

anchor: First principle: support and opposition must be separate ... S^+=0.9, S^-=0.8 does not mean S=0.1 ... There is substantial evidence on both sides. That is a conflict. ... Conflict(P) ... True if S^+>0 and S^->0 ... the conflict should retain C=(E^+,E^-,R,Ctx,Status)
statement: Requires support S+(P) and opposition S-(P) to be kept separate rather than collapsed to a net difference S=S+-S- (e.g. S+=0.9,S-=0.8 must not become S=0.1, since it hides substantial evidence on both sides); defines Conflict(P) as True when both are positive, retaining a structured conflict record (E+,E-,R,Ctx,Status).

anchor: Normalize evidence before aggregation ... N_\rho: \mathcal E\rightarrow\mathcal E' ... identity resolution; provenance resolution; semantic classification; relevance determination; temporal validity; dependency classification; polarity determination. ... Aggregation must occur after normalization. T
statement: Defines a normalization function N_ρ:E→E' performing identity resolution, provenance resolution, semantic classification, relevance determination, temporal validity, dependency classification, and polarity determination, and states the major architectural invariant: aggregation must occur only after normalization.

anchor: Evidence contribution is multidimensional ... q(e,P,C)=(r,q_s,q_r,q_t,q_c,q_p) ... Relevance ... Source quality ... Reliability ... Temporal validity ... Contextual applicability ... Provenance quality. This prevents us from collapsing fundamentally different properties. ... Highly authoritative / I
statement: Defines a six-dimension evidence-contribution vector q(e,P,C)=(r,q_s,q_r,q_t,q_c,q_p) — Relevance, Source quality, Reliability, Temporal validity, Contextual applicability, Provenance quality — illustrated with authoritative-but-irrelevant vs authoritative-and-relevant evidence to show a single scalar quality value would hide the difference; states Quality≠Relevance, Reliability≠Validity, ProvenanceQuality≠SourceAuthority.

anchor: The first mathematical operation: contribution filtering ... F_\rho(e,P,C) determines whether evidence is admissible ... F(e,P,C)=0 if Relevance(e,P,C)=0 ... irrelevant evidence contributes 0 but remains stored. ... NonContributing\neq Nonexistent
statement: Defines a contribution-filtering function F_ρ(e,P,C) that zeroes out irrelevant evidence's contribution to the current assessment while the evidence remains stored, giving the distinction NonContributing ≠ Nonexistent.

anchor: Dependency-adjusted contribution ... Document D ↓ LLM A ↓ Human report ... All three may support P, but their contributions are not simply additive. ... aggregation equivalence class [e]_{\sim_O} ... Same underlying observation is aggregated once unless policy explicitly states otherwise.
statement: Defines an aggregation equivalence class [e]~_O for evidence sharing the same underlying observation (e.g. Document D → LLM A → Human report, all supporting P), with the default rule that same-underlying-observation evidence is aggregated once unless policy states otherwise.

anchor: Independent corroboration ... e_1\perp_\rho e_2 ... Corroboration_\rho(e_1,e_2)>0 subject to the selected policy. This is where saturation or Bayesian models may become useful. But importantly: Corroboration is a policy operation, not a universal mathematical law.
statement: Defines Corroboration_ρ(e1,e2)>0 for operationally independent supporting evidence pairs, noting saturation or Bayesian models may apply, but insisting corroboration is a policy operation rather than a universal mathematical law.

anchor: What algebraic properties should aggregation have? ... Permutation invariance: Agg(e_1,e_2)=Agg(e_2,e_1) ... Duplicate invariance: e_1\sim_Oe_2 we require Agg(e_1,e_2)=Agg(e_1) ... Monotonicity: E\subseteq E' then Agg(E')\geq Agg(E) ... Boundedness: 0\leq Agg(E)\leq1 ... Dependency sensitivity: e_2\
statement: States five candidate algebraic properties for an aggregation operator Agg: permutation invariance (order-independence), duplicate invariance (same-observation pairs aggregate as one unless configured otherwise), monotonicity under added independent supporting evidence, boundedness (normalized measure in [0,1]), and dependency sensitivity (derived evidence must not add the same increment as an independent observation).

anchor: Important correction: not every useful assessment is monotonic ... e_1\Rightarrow P and then e_2\Rightarrow\neg P ... A support score for P should decrease if the assessment incorporates contradictory evidence. ... we should not demand universal monotonicity of the complete Evidence Assessment. ...
statement: Corrects the preceding monotonicity axiom: only SupportAggregation (aggregating supporting evidence alone) may be monotonic; the CompleteAssessment (incorporating contradictory evidence too) need not be monotonic, since discovering e2⇒¬P should legitimately decrease overall support for P.

anchor: Evidence Assessment is therefore not a scalar algebra ... EA_\rho: (\mathcal E,G_E,P,C)\rightarrow\mathcal A ... The scalar s\in[0,1] is merely one possible projection: \pi_s:\mathcal A\rightarrow[0,1]. This is a very important result. ... ScalarScore=\pi_\rho(EvidenceAssessment). This fits our earl
statement: Argues EA_ρ maps into a structured assessment space A (not a scalar algebra), with any scalar score s∈[0,1] arising only via a projection π_s:A→[0,1] — ScalarScore=π_ρ(EvidenceAssessment) — reaffirming that the scalar is derived, not fundamental.

anchor: DDD model ... EvidenceAssessment ... AssessmentId, Proposition, Context, SupportingEvidence, OpposingEvidence, DependencyGraph, QualityAssessment, UncertaintyAssessment, ValidityAssessment, AssessmentPolicy, AssessmentBasis, CreatedAt ... An EvidenceAssessment must preserve the evidential basis from
statement: Sketches the EvidenceAssessment aggregate (AssessmentId, Proposition, Context, SupportingEvidence, OpposingEvidence, DependencyGraph, QualityAssessment, UncertaintyAssessment, ValidityAssessment, AssessmentPolicy, AssessmentBasis, CreatedAt) with the invariant that it must preserve its evidential basis — never storing a bare confidence number without a reconstructible 'why'.

anchor: Assessment provenance ... Basis(EA)\subseteq \mathcal E ... Policy(EA)=\rho ... Context(EA)=C ... This gives us reproducibility: EA=f_\rho(E,C). The same evidence under a different policy may legitimately produce EA_{\rho_1}\neq EA_{\rho_2}
statement: Requires every EvidenceAssessment to carry Basis(EA)⊆E, Policy(EA)=ρ, and Context(EA)=C for reproducibility (EA=f_ρ(E,C)), noting the same evidence may legitimately yield different assessments under different policies.

anchor: Example — Nexus version ... Evidence 1 API ... Evidence 2 Filesystem ... Evidence 3 LLM summary of Evidence 1 ... Evidence 4 Old architecture document → 3.70 ... Supporting observations: API, Filesystem ... Derived support: LLM summary ... Opposing evidence: Old architecture document ... Assessment:
statement: Works a full Nexus-version worked example with four evidence items (API, filesystem, an LLM summary derived from the API, and a stale architecture document) producing a structured assessment (supporting/derived-support/opposing/dependency/temporal/conflict fields) explicitly contrasted with a bare scalar P(Nexus=3.69)=0.93 as containing far more information.

anchor: This gives us an important distinction ... EvidenceAssessment ... Conclusion ... Decision ... What does the evidence support? ... What proposition do we currently accept? ... What should we do? ... Evidence\rightarrow Assessment\rightarrow Conclusion\rightarrow Decision not Evidence\rightarrow Decis
statement: Distinguishes three domain concepts that must not be collapsed: Evidence Assessment (what does the evidence support?), Conclusion (what proposition do we currently accept?), and Decision (what should we do?) — mandating the pipeline Evidence→Assessment→Conclusion→Decision rather than a direct Evidence→Decision shortcut.

anchor: This is a major KnowledgeOS architectural boundary ... Evidence Context ... What evidence exists and how it relates. ... Assessment Context ... How evidence bears on a proposition. ... Knowledge Context ... What assertions are currently held in the Knowledge State. ... Decision Context ... What acti
statement: Defines four separate Context types as a major architectural boundary: Evidence Context (what evidence exists and how it relates), Assessment Context (how evidence bears on a proposition), Knowledge Context (what assertions the Knowledge State currently holds), and Decision Context (what action to take under a purpose/policy).

anchor: Where Zero fits ... Zero should not itself "decide truth." It detects EvidenceDeficiency, Conflict, InsufficientSupport, Staleness, UnknownDependency ... Zero: KnowledgeState + EvidenceAssessment + IdealState \rightarrow Findings
statement: Defines Zero's role as detecting EvidenceDeficiency, Conflict, InsufficientSupport, Staleness, and UnknownDependency (never deciding truth), formalized as Zero: KnowledgeState+EvidenceAssessment+IdealState → Findings.

anchor: Where Lord fits ... What additional evidence or knowledge would most reduce the discrepancy? ... Gap: Current version not independently verified through deployment inventory. ... Lord: Acquire deployment inventory evidence. This is much stronger than "Search for more information."
statement: Illustrates Lord's role — asking what additional evidence would most reduce a detected discrepancy, e.g. recommending 'acquire deployment inventory evidence' for an unverified version gap — as a much stronger recommendation than generic 'search for more information'.

anchor: Where Sarathi fits ... Sarathi takes (\Delta,EA,I,P) and determines the next appropriate action: Investigate, AcquireEvidence, ResolveConflict, RefreshEvidence, ClarifyContext, ReviseIdeal, AcceptUncertainty. ... Sarathi does not manufacture evidence.
statement: Defines Sarathi as taking (Δ, EvidenceAssessment, Ideal, Purpose) and choosing among seven action types (Investigate/AcquireEvidence/ResolveConflict/RefreshEvidence/ClarifyContext/ReviseIdeal/AcceptUncertainty), with the constraint that Sarathi does not manufacture evidence.

anchor:
Current mathematical status ... Established: Evidence
eq EvidenceAssessment ... EvidenceAssessment
eq Conclusion ... Conclusion
eq Decision ... Support^+
eq Support^- ... Aggregation
eq Inference ... Dependency must precede aggregation ... StructuredAssessment is fundamental. ... Still delibera
statement: Summarizes seven established distinctions/invariants (Evidence≠Assessment≠Conclusion≠Decision, Support+≠Support-, Aggregation≠Inference, Dependency-precedes-aggregation, StructuredAssessment-is-fundamental) and explicitly leaves the universal aggregation operator unselected as deliberately still open.

anchor: Step 4 — the next mathematical problem ... What properties must an Evidence Aggregation Operator satisfy, and which operators—max, mean, weighted sum, Dempster-Shafer, Bayesian, possibility theory, belief functions, etc.—satisfy them? ... Agg_\rho: \mathcal E^*\rightarrow\mathcal A subject to a set
statement: Poses Step 4: derive the required properties of an Evidence Aggregation Operator Agg_ρ:E*→A and test candidate frameworks (max, mean, weighted sum, Dempster-Shafer, Bayesian, possibility theory, belief functions) against KnowledgeOS axioms, via an axioms-first/counterexamples/candidate-testing method, to determine whether KnowledgeOS needs one evidence calculus or a family of admissible calculi.

lineage_claims.quote: That will tell us whether KnowledgeOS needs one evidence calculus or a family of admissible calculi.

anchor: First axiom: determinism ... EA_\rho(E,P,C)=EA_\rho(E,P,C) ... The same evidence, context and policy must produce the same assessment. If an LLM happens to produce different results each time, that variability cannot be hidden inside the mathematical definition. It must be represented as InferenceUn
statement: States the determinism axiom: fixed (evidence, proposition, context, policy) must produce the same EA_ρ; LLM output variability must be represented explicitly as InferenceUncertainty rather than hidden inside the aggregation function — LLM variability ≠ epistemic randomness.

anchor: Permutation invariance ... EA_\rho(\{e_1,e_2,e_3\},P,C) = EA_\rho(\{e_3,e_1,e_2\},P,C) ... The final assessment cannot depend merely on ingestion order.
statement: States the permutation-invariance axiom: the final EA must not depend on the order evidence was ingested (document today, database tomorrow, LLM result later, human review afterward).

anchor: Duplicate invariance ... e_1\equiv e_2 ... EA(E\cup\{e_1,e_2\}) = EA(E\cup\{e_1\}) ... prevents document duplication → artificial certainty. This should be a kernel invariant.
statement: States duplicate invariance — identical/equivalent evidence items must not increase the assessment beyond a single instance — flagged explicitly as a candidate kernel invariant preventing 'document duplication → artificial certainty'.

anchor: Derived-evidence non-inflation ... e_2=Transform(e_1) ... e_1\prec e_2 should imply IncrementalIndependentSupport(e_2\mid e_1)=0 unless the policy explicitly identifies an additional independent observation contained in e_2. This is particularly important for Document\rightarrow LLM\rightarrow Summa
statement: States the derived-evidence non-inflation axiom: if e2 is a transform of e1, its incremental independent support is 0 by default, unless policy identifies an additional independent observation within it — critical for Document→LLM→Summary→Report chains.

anchor: Irrelevance invariance ... Rel(e,P,C)=0 then EA(E\cup\{e\},P,C)=EA(E,P,C) ... The evidence is not deleted. It simply has no contribution ... NonRelevant\neq Nonexistent
statement: States irrelevance invariance: zero-relevance evidence leaves EA unchanged but is not deleted from the record — NonRelevant ≠ Nonexistent.

anchor: Supporting monotonicity ... e\Rightarrow P then S^+(E\cup\{e\})\ge S^+(E) ... e\Rightarrow\neg P implies S^-(E\cup\{e\})\ge S^-(E). This does not mean that the final conclusion must become more certain. Because new opposing evidence can simultaneously appear.
statement: States a refined monotonicity axiom applying separately to S+ and S- components (each only increases with admissible independent supporting/opposing evidence respectively), explicitly not implying the overall conclusion becomes more certain, since opposing evidence can appear simultaneously.

anchor: Contradiction preservation ... E^+\neq\emptyset and E^-\neq\emptyset then the assessment must retain both. EA(P)=(S^+,S^-,Conflict,\ldots) rather than EA(P)=singleScore ... S^+=0.91, S^-=0.88 must not become 0.03 because 0.03 conceals the existence of a serious conflict.
statement: States the contradiction-preservation axiom, called 'one of the most important axioms': when both supporting and opposing evidence exist, EA must retain both as structured fields rather than collapsing to a single net score, since e.g. S+=0.91,S-=0.88 collapsing to 0.03 would conceal a serious conflict.

anchor: Conflict sensitivity ... S^+>0 and S^->0 then Conflict(P)=Active subject to the conflict rule. ... Conflict_\rho(E^+,E^-,C) \rightarrow \{NoConflict,Potential,Active,Unresolved\} ... conflict detection is not simply arithmetic subtraction.
statement: Defines Conflict_ρ(E+,E-,C)→{NoConflict,Potential,Active,Unresolved} as a four-valued policy-governed function, stating conflict detection is not simple arithmetic subtraction.

anchor: Dependency sensitivity ... e_1\prec e_2 ... e_2 must not be treated as equivalent to an independent observation. Agg(E\cup\{e_2\}) \neq Agg(E\cup\{e_2^{independent}\}) ... This is a very strong test for candidate aggregation models.
statement: States dependency sensitivity as a strong test axiom: aggregating a dependent evidence item must differ from aggregating an otherwise-identical independent one (Agg(E∪{e2}) ≠ Agg(E∪{e2^independent})).

anchor: Unknown dependency must remain unknown ... Dependency(e_1,e_2)=Unknown ... cannot validly transform that into Independent(e_1,e_2)=True. UnknownDependency \Rightarrow No\ automatic\ independence\ credit. This does not mean UnknownDependency\Rightarrow Dependent. We retain Unknown. This is a three-va
statement: States that unknown dependency must remain Unknown throughout aggregation — no automatic independence credit, but also not automatically treated as Dependent — reaffirming the three-valued epistemic property from earlier files.

anchor: Corroboration ... e_1\perp_\rho e_2 and both support P, then the assessment should be capable of representing corroboration Corroboration_\rho(e_1,e_2)>0. But we deliberately do not specify Corroboration=0.4 yet. That is policy territory.
statement: States corroboration must be representable (Corroboration_ρ(e1,e2)>0 for independent, mutually supporting evidence) without fixing its numeric value, which remains policy territory.

anchor: Temporal sensitivity ... e_1 is current and e_2 is stale. We cannot treat them as identical. But Stale(e_2)\neq Delete(e_2). TemporalValidity affects contribution, not historical existence. ... A 2024 architecture document can still be valuable evidence about what existed in 2024, even if it is not
statement: States temporal sensitivity: stale evidence has reduced contribution but is never deleted (Stale ≠ Delete); temporal validity affects contribution, not historical existence — a 2024 document remains valid evidence about 2024 even if not about today.

anchor: Context sensitivity ... Contribution(e,P,C) ... Contribution(e,P,C_1) \neq Contribution(e,P,C_2) is perfectly legitimate. ... relevant to historical architecture reconstruction; irrelevant to a production migration decision; highly relevant to an audit of the 2024 environment. Evidence has no univer
statement: States context sensitivity: the same evidence can legitimately have different contributions in different contexts (illustrated by 'Nexus 3.69' being relevant/irrelevant/highly-relevant depending on the question asked) — 'Evidence has no universal relevance.'

anchor: Provenance preservation ... Basis(EA)\subseteq E ... EA\rightarrow EvidenceLineage must be recoverable. This gives us auditability. A KnowledgeOS conclusion should be able to answer "Why do you believe this?" with an actual evidence graph.
statement: States provenance preservation: EA must retain a recoverable evidence basis/lineage so a conclusion can answer 'Why do you believe this?' with an actual evidence graph.

anchor: No evidence creation ... E=\emptyset then Agg(E)=NoEvidence not Agg(E)=0.5 and certainly not Agg(E)=Confirmed. This is a critical distinction between absence of evidence and neutral evidence.
statement: States a no-evidence-creation axiom: aggregating the empty set must yield NoEvidence, never a neutral scalar (0.5) or Confirmed — distinguishing absence-of-evidence from neutral-evidence.

anchor: No certainty creation from aggregation alone ... StrongEvidence\not\Rightarrow Truth. Instead StrongEvidence \Rightarrow StrongSupport under the policy. Then another rule determines whether StrongSupport \Rightarrow AcceptedAssertion. That is a conclusion policy, not an evidence law.
statement: States StrongEvidence ⇏ Truth; strong evidence only yields StrongSupport under policy, and whether StrongSupport becomes an AcceptedAssertion is a separate conclusion-policy decision, not an evidence law.

anchor: This gives us three mathematical layers ... Layer A — Evidence aggregation E\rightarrow EA ... Layer B — Epistemic conclusion EA\rightarrow A ... Layer C — Decision A,I,P\rightarrow Decision ... Evidence\neq Conclusion\neq Decision
statement: Formalizes three mathematical layers — Layer A Evidence aggregation (E→EA), Layer B Epistemic conclusion (EA→A), Layer C Decision (A,Ideal,Purpose→Decision) — reaffirming Evidence ≠ Conclusion ≠ Decision.

anchor: Now we can define admissible aggregation ... Agg_\rho is admissible if it satisfies the applicable KnowledgeOS axioms \mathcal A=\{A_1,\ldots,A_n\} ... Agg_\rho\models\mathcal A ... This is the correct mathematical way to compare Bayesian, Dempster–Shafer, weighted, saturating, etc.
statement: Defines admissibility formally: Agg_ρ ⊨ A (satisfies the axiom set A) as the correct way to compare candidate frameworks (Bayesian, Dempster-Shafer, weighted, saturating).

anchor: But not every axiom must be universal ... kernel invariants: A_1 Identity preservation, A_2 Provenance preservation, A_3 Contradiction preservation, A_4 No automatic independence ... policy properties: A_5 Corroboration rule, A_6 Saturation, A_7 Decision threshold, A_8 Probability interpretation. Th
statement: Splits the axiom set into four kernel invariants (Identity preservation, Provenance preservation, Contradiction preservation, No automatic independence) versus four policy properties (Corroboration rule, Saturation, Decision threshold, Probability interpretation), called essential for DDD.

anchor: The emerging KnowledgeOS Evidence Constitution ... E-K1 — Evidence identity ... E-K2 — No duplicate inflation ... E-K3 — Provenance preservation ... E-K4 — Dependency awareness ... E-K5 — Unknown is not independent ... E-K6 — Contradiction preservation ... E-K7 — Context dependence ... E-K8 — Tempor
statement: Provisionally formulates a ten-item candidate 'KnowledgeOS epistemic constitution': E-K1 Evidence identity (e=e, explicitly represented), E-K2 No duplicate inflation, E-K3 Provenance preservation (Assessment⇒Basis), E-K4 Dependency awareness, E-K5 Unknown is not independent, E-K6 Contradiction preservation, E-K7 Context dependence, E-K8 Temporal preservation (Stale≠Deleted), E-K9 No truth by aggregation (EvidenceAssessment≠Truth), E-K10 No decision by aggregation (EvidenceAssessment≠Decision).

anchor: Now test candidate mathematics ... Maximum ... Avoids duplicate inflation ... Cannot represent cumulative corroboration well ... Mean ... Simple ... Duplicate-sensitive; dilution problems ... Weighted sum ... Flexible ... Weights become policy assumptions ... Bayesian ... Requires priors, likelihood
statement: Compares nine candidate aggregation frameworks (Maximum, Mean, Weighted sum, Saturating aggregation, Bayesian, Dempster-Shafer, Possibility theory, Argumentation frameworks, Graph-based evidence models) against strengths/problems, concluding there is probably no single universal KnowledgeOS evidence algebra — a Kernel + Pluggable Assessment Calculi architecture is mathematically stronger.

anchor: The architecture now looks like this ... RAW INPUTS → Evidence → Identity/Lineage/Dependency/Context/Validity → Evidence Graph → Assessment Calculus ρ → Evidence Assessment → Conclusion / Conflict → Knowledge State → Zero/Lord/Sarathi ... the calculus is a replaceable policy component.
statement: Diagrams the full pipeline from raw inputs through Evidence, identity/lineage/dependency/context/validity processing, an Evidence Graph, a replaceable Assessment Calculus ρ, Evidence Assessment, Conclusion/Conflict, Knowledge State, to Zero/Lord/Sārathi.

anchor: Step 4 conclusion ... We are no longer asking "Which formula gives the best confidence score?" We are asking "Which mathematical assessment calculi satisfy the epistemic and domain invariants of KnowledgeOS?" ... \mathcal C_{admissible} = \{\rho\mid Agg_\rho\models\mathcal A_{kernel}\} ... \mathcal
statement: Reframes Step 4's achievement as reformulating the question from 'best confidence formula' to 'which calculi satisfy KnowledgeOS's epistemic/domain invariants', formalized as the admissible-calculus set C_admissible={ρ | Agg_ρ⊨A_kernel}, with domain policies allowed to add axioms (A_ρ⊇A_kernel).

anchor: Step 5 — The next problem ... What exactly is the mathematical object being aggregated? Is it Evidence strength? Belief? Likelihood? Support? Arguments? Information gain? These are not interchangeable mathematical objects. ... Step 5 — Define the semantic domain of evidence contribution
statement: Poses Step 5's question — what mathematical object is actually being aggregated (evidence strength, belief, likelihood, support, arguments, or information gain — explicitly not interchangeable) — as a prerequisite before choosing between Bayesian, belief-function, possibility, or argumentation formalisms.

lineage_claims.quote: Step 5 -- Define the semantic domain of evidence contribution

anchor:
Until now we have deliberately used the generic word "support." We now need to determine what that actually means. ... Evidence 
eq Support 
eq Belief 
eq Probability 
eq Truth
statement: States that Evidence, Support, Belief, Probability, and Truth are different mathematical/domain concepts that must not be conflated under the generic word 'support'.

anchor: Start with the simplest object: a proposition ... An evidence object e does not itself need to be a proposition. ... These are artifacts or observations from which propositions may be extracted or supported. Evidence\ object\rightarrow Proposition is already an important transformation.
statement: Distinguishes propositions (P1: Nexus version=3.69, etc.) from evidence objects (API response, PDF, database row, screenshot, LLM output, ADR, etc.), which are artifacts/observations from which propositions are extracted, not propositions themselves; Evidence object → Proposition is itself a nontrivial transformation.

anchor: Evidence contribution ... c_\rho(e,P,C) ... the evidential contribution of e toward proposition P under context C and policy \rho. But we deliberately do not say c(e,P)\in[0,1] yet. That would prematurely impose a numerical interpretation.
statement: Defines the primitive c_ρ(e,P,C) — evidential contribution of e toward P under context C and policy ρ — deliberately withholding any commitment that its range is [0,1].

anchor: Why a scalar is dangerous ... c(e,P)=0.8 ... 80% probability ... strong evidential support; source reliability; confidence of an LLM; likelihood ratio; degree of belief; degree of plausibility; quality of the source. These are completely different things. 0.8 has no epistemic meaning until its seman
statement: Warns that an unlabeled scalar contribution value (e.g. 0.8) is dangerously ambiguous — it could mean probability, evidential support strength, source reliability, LLM confidence, likelihood ratio, degree of belief, plausibility, or source quality — and has no fixed epistemic meaning until its semantics are specified.

anchor: The semantic domains ... Reliability R(e) ... Relevance Rel(e,P,C) ... Evidential support Supp(e,P,C) ... Probability Pr(P\mid E,C) ... Belief Bel(P) ... Plausibility Pl(P) ... Information IG(E;P) ... How much did the evidence reduce uncertainty? Not: Is the proposition true?
statement: Enumerates seven distinct semantic domains that evidential contribution might mean: Reliability R(e), Relevance Rel(e,P,C), Evidential support Supp(e,P,C), Probability Pr(P|E,C), Belief Bel(P) (Dempster-Shafer sense, distinct from probability), Plausibility Pl(P), and Information IG(E;P) (uncertainty reduction, not truth).

anchor: Therefore we need an Evidence Contribution Domain ... \mathcal Q ... c_\rho: \mathcal E\times\mathcal P\times\mathcal C \rightarrow \mathcal Q ... Q does not have to be [0,1]. It might be an ordered scale; a vector; a belief function; a likelihood ratio; an argument structure; a set of possible stat
statement: Defines an Evidence Contribution Domain Q with c_ρ:E×P×C→Q, explicitly allowing Q to be an ordered scale, vector, belief function, likelihood ratio, argument structure, set of possible states, or probability distribution rather than fixed to [0,1].

anchor: My recommendation: the kernel should not choose one ... I would not put Bayesian probability or Dempster–Shafer belief into the KnowledgeOS kernel. KnowledgeOS Kernel = Evidence Semantics + Provenance + Relations ... Assessment Calculus = Pluggable Policy
statement: Recommends the kernel not commit to any specific probabilistic/belief framework: KnowledgeOS Kernel = Evidence Semantics + Provenance + Relations, while Assessment Calculus (Bayesian, Dempster-Shafer, Argumentation, Possibility, deterministic-rule, domain-specific) remains Pluggable Policy.

anchor: The most fundamental representation is therefore relational ... Rel(E,P) rather than Score(E,P). ... E1 → supports, E2 → supports, E3 → derived-from E1, E4 → contradicts, E5 → stale-supports. This relational structure is the epistemic foundation.
statement: Argues KnowledgeOS should first construct a relational structure Rel(E,P) (supports/derived-from/contradicts/stale-supports edges) rather than a Score(E,P) scalar, calling the relational structure the epistemic foundation.

anchor: Then assessment can be performed ... Assessment_\rho(P\mid E) ... Assessment_{Bayes}(P\mid E)=Pr(P\mid E) ... Assessment_{DS}(P\mid E)=(Bel(P),Pl(P)) ... Assessment_{Argument}(P\mid E)=Arguments^+(P),Arguments^-(P) ... These are not necessarily convertible into one universal number.
statement: Shows three concrete policy-specific instantiations of Assessment_ρ(P|E): Bayesian (Pr(P|E)), Dempster-Shafer ((Bel(P),Pl(P))), and Argumentation (Arguments+/-(P)), noting these are not necessarily convertible into one universal number.

anchor: This resolves an earlier problem ... Should KnowledgeOS use one evidence algebra? The answer is becoming clearer: No. The kernel should define what evidence means and how evidence relates. The reasoning policy determines how that evidence is mathematically assessed. This is a very strong DDD boundar
statement: Answers the recurring 'one evidence algebra?' question definitively No, drawing the DDD boundary: the kernel defines what evidence means and how it relates; the reasoning policy determines how it is mathematically assessed.

anchor: But we still need a common interface ... AssessmentResult ... AR=(P,Support,Opposition,Uncertainty,Basis,Context,Policy) ... Bayesian Support=Pr(P\mid E) ... Dempster-Shafer Support=Bel(P) ... Argumentation Support=accepted supporting arguments ... The domain object retains the semantics of the chos
statement: Proposes a common AssessmentResult interface AR=(P,Support,Opposition,Uncertainty,Basis,Context,Policy) whose Support field's internal representation differs by calculus (Bayesian probability, DS belief, argumentation's accepted arguments) while retaining that calculus's own semantics.

anchor: Important: "support" itself may need qualification ... EvidentialSupport from Acceptance ... Pr(P\mid E)=0.95 ... 0.95\Rightarrow Accepted ... Another may require 0.99\Rightarrow Accepted. Assessment\neq Acceptance. Acceptance is a policy decision.
statement: Distinguishes EvidentialSupport from Acceptance: different policies may set different acceptance thresholds on the same support value (e.g. 0.95 vs 0.99), so Assessment ≠ Acceptance — acceptance is a policy decision.

anchor: And acceptance is not truth ... Accepted(P) does not mean Truth(P). Accepted(P) = currently accepted under policy \rho. This is precisely the distinction our Knowledge State needs.
statement: States Accepted(P) ≠ Truth(P); Accepted(P) means only 'currently accepted under policy ρ', a distinction needed by the Knowledge State.

anchor: The statistical interpretation ... Pr(P\mid E) = Pr(E\mid P)Pr(P)/Pr(E) ... we need prior; likelihood; evidence model; dependency assumptions; sampling assumptions; model adequacy. KnowledgeOS cannot simply infer these from the existence of a document. Probability requires a model.
statement: Notes Bayesian Pr(P|E) requires priors, likelihoods, an evidence model, dependency and sampling assumptions, and model adequacy that cannot be inferred merely from a document's existence — 'Probability requires a model.'

anchor: Example: two documents ... A naive system might say 2 confirmations. But our model asks Dependency(A,B)=? If A\rightarrow B then IndependentEvidenceCount=1. If A\perp B then they may provide two contributions. If Dependency(A,B)=Unknown then we do not pretend to know.
statement: Worked example: two documents both stating 'Nexus 3.69' naively look like two confirmations, but the correct count depends on Dependency(A,B) — 1 if dependent, 2 if independently acquired, and an honest 'we do not pretend to know' if Dependency is Unknown.

anchor: The evidence contribution should therefore be factored ... c_\rho(e,P,C)=g_\rho(Rel,Qual,Relia,Valid,Context,Dependency,Polarity) ... g_\rho is policy-specific. The kernel stores the dimensions. The policy determines how they combine.
statement: Factors evidence contribution as c_ρ(e,P,C)=g_ρ(Relevance,Quality,Reliability,Validity,Context,Dependency,Polarity), where the kernel stores the seven dimensions and the policy-specific function g_ρ determines how they combine.

anchor: This gives us a very clean mathematical decomposition ... Evidence semantics ... Evidence relation ... Proposition relation ... Assessment ... Conclusion ... Knowledge State ... E\rightarrow Relations\rightarrow Assessment\rightarrow Conclusion\rightarrow KnowledgeState
statement: Assembles the full pipeline E→Relations→Assessment→Conclusion→KnowledgeState across six named mappings (Evidence semantics, Evidence relation, Proposition relation, Assessment, Conclusion, Knowledge State update).

anchor: DDD interpretation ... Evidence ... EvidenceRelation ... PropositionAssessment ... Conclusion ... KnowledgeState ... Decision ... These should not be one aggregate.
statement: Names six DDD concepts (Evidence, EvidenceRelation, PropositionAssessment, Conclusion, KnowledgeState, Decision) that must remain separate aggregates rather than merged into one.

anchor: Now let's examine candidate mathematics ... Weighted arithmetic ... 0.8 has no universal epistemic semantics. ... Saturating aggregation ... 1-\prod(1-s_i) does not itself solve dependency. It requires our Evidence Graph first. ... Bayesian ... Not universal. ... Dempster-Shafer ... its combination
statement: Re-examines candidate calculi against the semantic-domain requirement: weighted arithmetic's 0.8 still lacks universal semantics; saturating aggregation (1-∏(1-s_i)) does not itself resolve dependency without the Evidence Graph; Bayesian and Dempster-Shafer each carry their own assumptions; argumentation uniquely preserves why an assertion is supported/attacked.

anchor: A significant insight ... KnowledgeOS may need two complementary mathematical families. Quantitative evidence calculus ... Bayesian, Statistical, Possibility ... Qualitative/argumentative calculus ... ADR-001 supports decision A, ADR-002 attacks assumption X ... Not every epistemic problem should be
statement: Argues KnowledgeOS needs two complementary calculus families — quantitative (Bayesian/Statistical/Possibility) for numerically meaningful uncertainty, and qualitative/argumentative (for ADRs, architectural principles, competing interpretations) — proposing the principle 'Not every epistemic problem should become a probability problem.'

anchor: Our current formal model ... \mathcal E = Evidence Universe ... \mathcal P = Proposition Universe ... \mathcal C = Context Universe ... \mathcal R_E = Evidence Relations ... Assessment_\rho: (\mathcal E,\mathcal R_E,\mathcal P,\mathcal C) \rightarrow \mathcal A_\rho
statement: Consolidates the formal model: Evidence Universe E, Proposition Universe P, Context Universe C, Evidence Relations R_E, and Assessment_ρ:(E,R_E,P,C)→A_ρ where A_ρ is the policy-defined assessment space.

anchor: What belongs to the immutable kernel? ... KERNEL = {Evidence, Proposition, Provenance, Lineage, Dependency, Context, TemporalValidity, Polarity, AssessmentBasis} ... POLICY = {Aggregation, Inference, Thresholds, ProbabilityModels, BeliefModels, DecisionRules}. This separation is architecturally extr
statement: Proposes a nine-item KERNEL vocabulary (Evidence, Proposition, Provenance, Lineage, Dependency, Context, TemporalValidity, Polarity, AssessmentBasis) versus a six-item POLICY vocabulary (Aggregation, Inference, Thresholds, ProbabilityModels, BeliefModels, DecisionRules) as an architecturally clean separation.

anchor: One more important issue: information gain ... P(Nexus=3.69)=0.5 ... P(Nexus=3.69)=0.99 ... InformationGain from EvidenceStrength. A weak piece of evidence can sometimes have enormous information value if it resolves a previously critical uncertainty. EvidenceValue\neq EvidenceStrength. This will be
statement: Introduces InformationGain as distinct from EvidenceStrength, illustrated by a probability shift from 0.5 to 0.99: a weak piece of evidence can have enormous information value if it resolves a critical uncertainty — EvidenceValue ≠ EvidenceStrength, foreshadowing Lord/Sarathi's evidence-acquisition selection.

anchor: Step 5 verdict ... Theoretical status: substantially resolved ... The fundamental object is not a scalar score. Evidence Contribution is a policy-interpreted semantic relation. Assessment is a structured object. Probability, belief, likelihood, information gain and argument strength are different ma
statement: Declares Step 5 'substantially resolved': the fundamental object is not a scalar score; Evidence Contribution is a policy-interpreted semantic relation; Assessment is a structured object; probability/belief/likelihood/information-gain/argument-strength are different mathematical constructs.

anchor: Next: Step 6 — Information Gain and Value of Evidence ... If KnowledgeOS already knows some things and has gaps, how does it determine which new evidence would be most valuable to acquire? Value(e\mid K,I,P) ... e^* = \arg\max_e ExpectedDiscrepancyReduction(e) ... Lord and Sarathi begin to acquire a
statement: Poses Step 6: define Value(e|K,I,P) and e*=argmax_e ExpectedDiscrepancyReduction(e) so Lord/Sarathi can select the next evidence acquisition that most reduces uncertainty/discrepancy, rather than merely 'find more evidence'.

lineage_claims.quote: Next: Step 6 -- Information Gain and Value of Evidence

anchor: The fundamental distinction ... Evidence Strength \neq Information Gain \neq Decision Value ... How strongly does an evidence item support a proposition? ... How much does the evidence reduce uncertainty? ... How much does acquiring the evidence improve the decision?
statement: Separates three related-but-distinct quantities: Evidence Strength (support magnitude), Information Gain (uncertainty reduction), and Decision Value (improvement to the decision from acquiring the evidence).

anchor: Can Nexus be migrated safely? ... Version = 3.69 ... Knowing the exact patch version may add little information. ... Is the production blob store backed up? ... may currently be completely unknown. A single answer could dramatically reduce the migration uncertainty. Highest Evidence Strength \neq Hi
statement: Illustrates with a migration-safety question that a strongly-evidenced fact (Nexus version) can add little new information, while an unknown backup-status question could dramatically reduce uncertainty with a single answer — Highest Evidence Strength ≠ Highest Information Gain.

anchor: Information gain in information theory ... H(P) = -\sum_x P(x)\log P(x) ... P(P)=0.5 then H(P)=1 bit ... P(P\mid e)=0.95 and H(P\mid e)<H(P) ... IG(e;P) = H(P)-H(P\mid e). This is a mathematically rigorous definition of information gain.
statement: Defines entropy-based information gain IG(e;P)=H(P)-H(P|e) using Shannon entropy H(P)=-Σ P(x)log P(x), worked with a 0.5→0.95 probability update as a rigorous but calculus-specific definition.

anchor: But this is not universal ... Entropy requires a probabilistic representation. ... unknown values; logical constraints; competing assertions; qualitative uncertainty; argument graphs; incomplete evidence. Therefore we should not define IG=EntropyReduction as a universal KnowledgeOS law. InformationG
statement: Corrects the previous entropy definition's universality: entropy requires a probabilistic representation, which KnowledgeOS often lacks (unknown values, logical constraints, argument graphs), so IG=EntropyReduction must not be a universal law — InformationGain_ρ is policy-specific.

anchor: General definition ... discrepancy function D(S,I,P) ... IG_D(e) = D(S_t,I_t,P) - D(S_{t+1}^{(e)},I_t,P) ... Information gain can be measured as reduction in discrepancy.
statement: Generalizes information gain beyond entropy: IG_D(e)=D(S_t,I_t,P)-D(S_{t+1}^(e),I_t,P), i.e. information gain measured as reduction in a discrepancy function relative to the Ideal State.

anchor: But there is an important complication ... We usually don't know in advance what evidence e will reveal. ... Yes; No; Unknown; "Backups exist but have never been tested." Therefore we need expected information gain. ... EIG(e) = \sum_{o\in O_e} Pr(o\mid e,K_t)[D(K_t,I_t,P)-D(K_{t+1}^{o},I_t,P)]
statement: Notes evidence outcomes are unknown in advance (e.g. a yes/no/unknown/qualified backup-status answer), requiring Expected Information Gain EIG(e)=Σ_o Pr(o|e,K_t)[D(K_t,I_t,P)-D(K_{t+1}^o,I_t,P)] over possible outcomes o.

anchor: Expected discrepancy reduction ... EDR(e) = \mathbb E[D(K_t,I_t,P)-D(K_{t+1},I_t,P)\mid e] ... This does not require us to call it information theory. It can be used with deterministic gap counts; probabilistic uncertainty; belief functions; argumentation; domain-specific discrepancy measures.
statement: Defines Expected Discrepancy Reduction EDR(e)=E[D(K_t,I_t,P)-D(K_{t+1},I_t,P)|e], deliberately framework-neutral so it can be instantiated with deterministic gap counts, probability, belief functions, argumentation, or other domain-specific discrepancy measures.

anchor: This is probably more fundamental for KnowledgeOS ... ExpectedDiscrepancyReduction more fundamental than EntropyReduction ... KnowledgeOS is not merely trying to reduce uncertainty. It is trying to move K_t toward I_t. Therefore the natural objective is K_t\rightarrow I_t and not merely H(K_t)\right
statement: Argues ExpectedDiscrepancyReduction is more fundamental to KnowledgeOS than EntropyReduction, since KnowledgeOS's real objective is moving K_t toward I_t, not merely driving entropy to zero.

anchor: A critical counterexample ... P(A)=0.5 and P(B)=0.5 ... A is irrelevant to the current decision. Then IG(A)>0 but EDR(A)\approx0. Meanwhile evidence about B might directly resolve a Critical Gap. InformationGain\neq PurposeValue. This is why purpose P must remain in the equation.
statement: Gives a counterexample where entropy-reducing evidence about an irrelevant proposition A has high IG but near-zero EDR, while evidence about a decision-relevant proposition B would resolve a critical gap — InformationGain ≠ PurposeValue, so purpose must remain in the equation.

anchor: Value of Evidence ... VOE_\rho(e\mid K_t,I_t,P,C) ... the expected value of acquiring evidence e ... VOE(e) = ExpectedDiscrepancyReduction(e) \times DecisionImpact(e) ... this multiplication is not a universal law. It is one possible policy.
statement: Defines Value of Evidence VOE_ρ(e|K_t,I_t,P,C) as the expected value of acquiring e, offering EDR(e)×DecisionImpact(e) as one possible (non-universal) policy decomposition.

anchor: Cost must also be included ... Evidence A ... 0.9 ... €10,000 ... Evidence B ... 0.7 ... €10 ... Clearly, "maximum information gain" alone is insufficient. We need Cost(e) and potentially Time(e), Risk(e), Effort(e)
statement: Shows via a cost/benefit contrast (Evidence A: EDR 0.9 at €10,000 vs Evidence B: EDR 0.7 at €10) that maximizing information gain alone is insufficient — Cost, Time, Risk, and Effort must also enter the evaluation.

anchor: Utility of evidence ... U_\rho(e) = Benefit_\rho(e) - Cost_\rho(e) ... U(e) = \alpha EDR(e) + \beta DecisionImpact(e) - \gamma Cost(e) - \delta Time(e) ... the coefficients \alpha,\beta,\gamma,\delta are policy parameters. They are not mathematical truths.
statement: Defines evidence utility U_ρ(e)=Benefit_ρ(e)-Cost_ρ(e), with a worked linear form U(e)=αEDR(e)+βDecisionImpact(e)-γCost(e)-δTime(e) whose coefficients are explicitly labeled policy parameters, not mathematical truths.

anchor: The evidence acquisition problem ... \mathcal Q ... Q1 = inspect filesystem ... Q8 = ask LLM to extract information ... q^* = \arg\max_{q\in\mathcal Q} U_\rho(q\mid K_t,I_t,P) ... This is potentially one of the most important equations in the whole KnowledgeOS theory.
statement: Formalizes Lord's core problem as q*=argmax_{q∈Q} U_ρ(q|K_t,I_t,P) over a candidate acquisition-action set Q (inspect filesystem, query API, read document, ask engineer, inspect backup config, run test, search internet, ask LLM) — called potentially one of the most important equations in the whole theory.

anchor: Lord's role becomes precise ... Lord(K_t,I_t,P,\rho) \rightarrow RankedCandidateAcquisitions ... Candidate 1 Inspect production backup configuration Expected discrepancy reduction: High Cost: Low Risk: Low
statement: Formalizes Lord as Lord(K_t,I_t,P,ρ)→RankedCandidateAcquisitions, illustrated with a ranked candidate list (inspect backup config / ask infra owner / search internet) each carrying EDR/Cost/Risk estimates.

anchor: Sarathi then chooses or guides ... Lord generates the candidate space. Sārathi considers current constraints; available capabilities; urgency; policy; safety; dependencies; human authority. Sārathi : Candidates \rightarrow NextAction ... Lord = option generation/ranking ... Sārathi = action guidance
statement: Distinguishes Lord (option generation/ranking) from Sārathi (Candidates→NextAction, factoring in constraints/urgency/policy/safety/dependencies/human authority) as separate roles.

anchor: Zero has a different role ... Zero(K_t,I_t) \rightarrow \Delta_t ... Lord(\Delta_t) \rightarrow Q ... Sārathi(Q,constraints) \rightarrow a_t ... This gives us a very elegant cycle: Knowledge K_t → Zero → Δ_t → Lord → candidates → Sārathi → action → Evidence Acquisition → New Knowledge K_t+1 → Zero
statement: Assembles the full Zero→Lord→Sārathi cycle: Zero(K_t,I_t)→Δ_t, Lord(Δ_t)→Q (candidates), Sārathi(Q,constraints)→a_t (action), producing new evidence and K_{t+1}, feeding back into Zero.

anchor: This is much more than RAG ... Question \rightarrow Retrieve \rightarrow Generate ...
