Purpose \rightarrow IdealState \rightarrow Discrepancy \rightarrow EvidenceValue \rightarrow AcquisitionPlan \rightarrow Evidence \rightarrow Assessment \rightarrow KnowledgeState. That is a fundamentally different
statement: Contrasts traditional RAG's Question→Retrieve→Generate pipeline with KnowledgeOS's Purpose→IdealState→Discrepancy→EvidenceValue→AcquisitionPlan→Evidence→Assessment→KnowledgeState pipeline as a fundamentally different architecture.

anchor: Human research fits naturally ... q=HumanInquiry ... HumanResponse\rightarrow Evidence ... Acquisition=Reported ... Source=Human ... The human's statement does not automatically become truth. It enters exactly the same evidence machinery.
statement: Shows human inquiry fits the same acquisition/evidence machinery (q=HumanInquiry → HumanResponse→Evidence with Acquisition=Reported, Source=Human), with the human's statement not automatically becoming truth.

anchor: LLM output also fits ... LLM(D)\rightarrow e ... Acquisition=Inferred ... Parent=D ... LLMOutput\neq GroundTruth ... LLMOutput\neq IndependentEvidence when it derives from existing evidence. This is one of the major architectural strengths of the model.
statement: Shows LLM output fits the same graph (LLM(D)→e with Acquisition=Inferred, Parent=D), reaffirming LLMOutput ≠ GroundTruth and LLMOutput ≠ IndependentEvidence when derived from existing evidence.

anchor: Experimental evidence ... Hypothesis: Nexus backup can be restored. Experiment: Restore backup to isolated environment. Observation: Restore succeeded. Evidence: e_exp ... Acquisition(e)=Observed with provenance Experiment\rightarrow Observation. This can have much higher relevance to a migration de
statement: Models experimental evidence (Hypothesis/Experiment/Observation/Evidence, e.g. restoring a backup to an isolated environment) with Acquisition=Observed and provenance Experiment→Observation, noted as potentially higher relevance than a textual claim.

anchor: Expected value versus actual value ... ExpectedValue(e) ... ActualDiscrepancyReduction(e) ... These must not be confused. An investigation can be expected to be extremely valuable but turn out to provide no useful information. ExpectedValue\neq ActualValue.
statement: Distinguishes ExpectedValue(e) (before acquisition) from ActualDiscrepancyReduction(e) (after), noting an investigation can be expected to be valuable yet turn out useless.

anchor: This creates a feedback loop ... K_t\rightarrow K_{t+1} then \Delta_t\rightarrow\Delta_{t+1}. Now KnowledgeOS can recalculate VOE(e) for remaining candidate actions. (K_t,I_t,\Delta_t) \rightarrow q_t \rightarrow e_t \rightarrow K_{t+1}
statement: Formalizes the iterative feedback loop (K_t,I_t,Δ_t)→q_t→e_t→K_{t+1}, with VOE recalculated for remaining candidates after each acquisition.

anchor: Stopping condition ... When should KnowledgeOS stop acquiring evidence? ... \Delta_t\leq\epsilon ... only works if discrepancy has a meaningful scalar or ordering. ... \forall q\in Q: U_\rho(q)\leq U_{\min} ... AcceptCurrentState ... AcceptUncertainty ... Unresolvable. This is much more realistic.
statement: Defines a stopping condition more general than a scalar threshold Δ_t≤ε: when no candidate action has sufficient expected utility (∀q: U_ρ(q)≤U_min), recommending AcceptCurrentState, AcceptUncertainty, or Unresolvable as outcomes.

anchor: Critical mathematical distinction ... We should not define Moksha = \Delta=0 or anything similar as a mathematical consequence of this framework. Our model allows \Delta\rightarrow0 for a specified purpose and context, but not necessarily globally. ... \Delta=0 always means only relative to the spec
statement: Explicitly warns against defining any global metaphysical end-state (e.g. 'Moksha=Δ=0') as a consequence of the framework: Δ=0 is always only relative to a specified purpose/context ideal, never a global claim — flagged as an important mathematical safeguard.

anchor: Our new formal layer ... Q_t=\{q_1,\ldots,q_n\} ... EDR(q) ... U_\rho(q)=Benefit_\rho(q)-Cost_\rho(q) ... q^* = \arg\max_{q\in Q_t}U_\rho(q) ... K_{t+1} = \delta(K_t,Acquire(q^*))
statement: Consolidates the formal layer: candidate acquisitions Q_t, EDR(q), utility U_ρ(q), optimal next acquisition q*=argmax U_ρ(q), and resulting transition K_{t+1}=δ(K_t,Acquire(q*)).

anchor: The KnowledgeOS decision loop ... 1. K_t 2. Zero(K_t,I_t)\rightarrow\Delta_t 3. GenerateCandidates(\Delta_t)\rightarrow Q_t 4. EvaluateValue(Q_t,K_t,I_t,P,\rho) 5. q^*=\arg\max U_\rho(q) 6. Acquire(q^*)\rightarrow e_t 7. Assess(e_t) 8. Update(K_t,e_t)\rightarrow K_{t+1} 9. Repeat. This is the beginn
statement: Assembles the full nine-step KnowledgeOS decision loop algorithm (K_t → Zero → Δ_t → GenerateCandidates → Q_t → EvaluateValue → q* → Acquire → Assess → Update → K_{t+1} → Repeat), called the beginning of an active epistemic system.

anchor: Step 6 verdict ... THEORETICALLY RESOLVED ... The exact EDR and U_\rho functions are policy/calculus dependent. We do not need to resolve them universally. The kernel only needs to provide the abstraction EvidenceValueEvaluator with domain-specific implementations.
statement: Declares Step 6 theoretically resolved with the qualification that EDR and U_ρ remain policy/calculus-dependent; the kernel need only provide an EvidenceValueEvaluator abstraction with domain-specific implementations.

anchor: What we have now ... Evidence\rightarrow EvidenceRelations\rightarrow Assessment\rightarrow Discrepancy\rightarrow CandidateAcquisition\rightarrow NewEvidence ... KnowledgeOS is potentially an active knowledge acquisition system rather than merely a knowledge storage/retrieval system.
statement: Summarizes the theory's evolution into a full pipeline (Evidence→EvidenceRelations→Assessment→Discrepancy→CandidateAcquisition→NewEvidence), concluding KnowledgeOS is potentially an active knowledge acquisition system, not merely storage/retrieval.

anchor: Step 7 — The next mathematical question ... How does a newly acquired piece of evidence actually change the Knowledge State? K_t + e \rightarrow K_{t+1} ... new assertions; updated assertions; superseded assertions; contradictions; gaps becoming resolved; new gaps appearing; evidence becoming stale;
statement: Poses Step 7: fully specify the Knowledge State transition K_{t+1}=δ(K_t,e_t) covering new/updated/superseded assertions, contradictions, gap resolution/emergence, staleness, retraction, provenance and temporal versioning — called 'the mathematical heart of the KnowledgeOS kernel' to be resolved before any implementation.

lineage_claims.quote: this transition mechanism is essentially the mathematical heart of the KnowledgeOS kernel

anchor: The fundamental problem ... A naive model would say K_{t+1}=K_t\cup e_t. That is insufficient. ... introduce a new assertion; strengthen; weaken; contradict; resolve a conflict; create a new conflict; invalidate; make stale; change an interpretation; expose that a previous conclusion was unsupported
statement: Rejects the naive model K_{t+1}=K_t∪e_t as insufficient, listing eleven distinct effects new evidence can have (introduce/strengthen/weaken/contradict/resolve/create conflict/invalidate/stale/reinterpret/expose unsupported/reveal new dimension) to establish K_{t+1}≠K_t∪e_t in general.

anchor: What exactly is the Knowledge State? ... K_t=(\mathcal A_t,\mathcal E_t,\mathcal R_t,\mathcal C_t,\mathcal H_t,\Gamma_t) ... Assertions currently represented ... Evidence known to the system ... Relations between knowledge objects ... Active conflicts ... Historical event/state record ... Current co
statement: Defines the Knowledge State as a six-component tuple K_t=(Assertions, Evidence, Relations, ActiveConflicts, History, ContextualConditions), holding not just beliefs but the structure explaining why/under-what-conditions they are held.

anchor: Current state versus history ... K_t \neq H_t ... An assertion may no longer be current while remaining historically important. ... 2024: Nexus = 3.69 ... 2025: Nexus = 3.70 ... 2026: Nexus = 3.85 ... Superseded\neq Deleted
statement: Distinguishes current Knowledge State K_t from historical evolution H_t, illustrated by three successive Nexus-version assertions, concluding Superseded ≠ Deleted.

anchor: Knowledge State transition ... K_{t+1} = \delta_\rho(K_t,e_t) ... the actual transition should be mediated by an epistemic event: K_t \xrightarrow{event_t} K_{t+1} because evidence itself does not directly mutate knowledge.
statement: Refines the transition K_{t+1}=δ_ρ(K_t,e_t) to be mediated by an explicit epistemic event rather than evidence directly mutating knowledge.

anchor: Evidence does not directly change knowledge ... We do not automatically execute K:=K\cup\{Nexus=3.69\}. Instead e \rightarrow Assessment \rightarrow Conclusion \rightarrow KnowledgeStateTransition. Evidence\not\Rightarrow Knowledge ... Evidence \rightarrow EvidenceAssessment \rightarrow EpistemicCon
statement: States the crucial invariant Evidence ⇏ Knowledge: evidence must pass through Assessment and Conclusion stages before touching the Knowledge State, preventing raw LLM output/documents/human statements from silently becoming accepted knowledge.

anchor: The transition pipeline ... e_t \rightarrow EA_t \rightarrow c_t \rightarrow \delta_\rho \rightarrow K_{t+1}
statement: Formalizes the transition pipeline e_t→EA_t (Evidence Assessment)→c_t (conclusion/update proposal)→δ_ρ (state transition policy)→K_{t+1}.

anchor: What operations can happen? ... Introduce(P,e)\rightarrow A ... Corroborate(A,e)\rightarrow A' ... Qualify ... Nexus 3.69 in the legacy environment ... Contradict(A,e)\rightarrow Conflict ... Supersede ... TemporalChange\neq LogicalContradiction ... Resolve(C)\rightarrow ContextualizedAssertions rat
statement: Defines eight named Knowledge-State transition operations: Introduce (new proposition represented), Corroborate (independent supporting evidence strengthens an assertion), Qualify (adds conditions without invalidating), Contradict (produces Conflict, not automatic replacement), Supersede (temporal change ≠ logical contradiction), Resolve (produces contextualized assertions, never silent deletion), Retract (retract ≠ delete, retaining historical status/evidence/provenance), and Invalidate (temporal expiry ≠ retraction).

anchor: The transition algebra ... \mathcal O_K=\{Introduce,Corroborate,Qualify,Contradict,Supersede,Resolve,Retract,Invalidate\} ... \delta: K\times\mathcal O_K \rightharpoonup K ... The arrow is partial ... because not every operation is valid in every state. ... Resolve(C) is invalid if C\notin\mathcal C
statement: Formalizes the transition algebra δ:K×O_K⇀K as a partial function over the eight-operation set O_K, since not every operation is valid in every state (e.g. Resolve(C) is invalid unless C is an active conflict).

anchor: This gives us state-machine semantics ... Do not make this a single linear lifecycle. An assertion's epistemic dimensions are independent. ... State = (Acquisition,Support,Uncertainty,Validity) plus relational state: Conflict, Resolution, Supersession, etc.
statement: Rejects a single linear assertion lifecycle (Unknown→Introduced→Corroborated/Conflicted/Retracted/Superseded) as inadequate since an assertion's epistemic dimensions are independent, proposing instead an independent-dimension State=(Acquisition,Support,Uncertainty,Validity) plus separate relational state (Conflict/Resolution/Supersession).

anchor: Therefore assertion state remains multidimensional ... \Sigma_A=(Acquisition,Support,Uncertainty,Validity) ... (Observed,Strong,Low,Current) could become (Observed,Strong,Low,Stale) without changing support. ... a single lifecycle such as Observed → Confirmed → Resolved is mathematically inadequate.
statement: Illustrates the multidimensional assertion state Σ_A=(Acquisition,Support,Uncertainty,Validity) with an example where only Validity changes (Current→Stale) while Support stays unchanged, confirming a single linear lifecycle is mathematically inadequate.

anchor: State transition as a delta ... \Delta\Sigma = \Sigma_{t+1}-\Sigma_t ... Before: Support = Moderate, Validity = Current ... Event: Independent filesystem observation ... After: Support = Strong, Validity = Current ... The exact algebra of +1 is policy-specific; the important thing is that the change
statement: Defines state transitions as an explicit delta ΔΣ=Σ_{t+1}-Σ_t over the multidimensional state, worked with a Support Moderate→Strong example, noting the exact delta algebra is policy-specific but the changed dimensions must be explicit.

anchor: Event sourcing becomes mathematically natural ... H_t=(e_1,e_2,\ldots,e_t) ... K_t=Fold(\delta,H_t,K_0) ... K_t = \delta(\ldots\delta(\delta(K_0,e_1),e_2)\ldots,e_t) ... This gives us reproducibility.
statement: Formalizes event-sourced reconstruction K_t=Fold(δ,H_t,K_0), i.e. K_t as the iterated application of δ over the event history from K_0, giving reproducibility.

anchor: But there is an important problem ... State reconstruction must be deterministic for a fixed initial state; event history; policy version; knowledge ontology/schema version. K_t = F(K_0,H_t,\rho,\omega)
statement: Requires state reconstruction to be deterministic given a fixed initial state, event history, policy version ρ, and ontology/schema version ω: K_t=F(K_0,H_t,ρ,ω).

anchor: Why policy version matters ... 2026 Threshold=0.90 means accepted. In 2027 Threshold=0.95. The same evidence may produce different conclusions under the two policies. Therefore we must preserve PolicyVersion with the assessment/conclusion. Otherwise historical reconstruction becomes ambiguous.
statement: Argues policy version must be preserved with every assessment/conclusion, since a threshold change (e.g. 0.90→0.95) makes the same evidence yield different conclusions across time, and omitting it makes historical reconstruction ambiguous.

anchor: Why ontology version matters ... SecurityStatus changes. Then an old conclusion may not be interpretable under the new semantic model. Therefore SemanticModelVersion or equivalent provenance is necessary. This is especially important for KnowledgeOS because the ontology itself may evolve.
statement: Argues a SemanticModelVersion (or equivalent provenance) must also be preserved, since changes to a concept's meaning (e.g. SecurityStatus) can make old conclusions uninterpretable under a newer ontology.

anchor: Temporal state ... t_{acquisition} ... t_{validity} ... t_{knowledge} ... A document written in 2024 is uploaded to KnowledgeOS in 2026 ... t_{source}=2024 ... t_{acquisition}=2026 ... t_{knowledge state}=2026 ... ValidAt=2024. Knowledge time\neq Source time\neq Validity time
statement: Distinguishes three time axes (source time, acquisition time, knowledge-state time) using a 2024 document uploaded in 2026: t_source=2024, t_acquisition=2026, t_knowledge=2026, ValidAt=2024 — Knowledge time ≠ Source time ≠ Validity time, essential for architecture reconstruction.

anchor: Current state and historical state ... K_t(P,C) as the current knowledge regarding proposition P in context C. And K_{[t_1,t_2]} as the historical state over a time interval. ... What is true/currently accepted now? and What did we know / believe / observe at that time? Those must not be confused.
statement: Formally separates current knowledge K_t(P,C) from historical-interval knowledge K_[t1,t2], so 'what is currently accepted' and 'what did we believe at time t' are never confused.

anchor: Retraction and belief revision ... A_1:P is accepted. Later e_2:\neg P. If we simply remove P, we lose history. If we retain both as current truths, we may introduce inconsistency. Therefore KnowledgeOS needs belief revision semantics. Status(A)\in\{Active,Superseded,Retracted,Expired,Contested,Hist
statement: Argues KnowledgeOS needs belief-revision semantics rather than either deleting a contradicted assertion or keeping both as current truths, defining a six-value Status(A) enum {Active,Superseded,Retracted,Expired,Contested,Historical}.

anchor: We should avoid classical explosion ... P and \neg P ... classical logic would allow P\land\neg P and under unrestricted classical inference potentially derive arbitrary propositions. That would be catastrophic. KnowledgeOS therefore needs a paraconsistent stance toward contradictory knowledge. Conf
statement: Adopts an explicit paraconsistent stance: KnowledgeOS must avoid classical explosion (P∧¬P deriving arbitrary propositions under classical logic), representing contradictions via a first-class Conflict object instead of unrestricted classical inference.

anchor: Knowledge State is therefore a contradiction-tolerant structure ... K_t=\{P,\neg P\} with Conflict(P,\neg P)=Active. Then K_t remains usable. Zero detects the conflict. Lord identifies what evidence could resolve it. Sārathi determines whether resolution is necessary before action.
statement: Represents K_t as a contradiction-tolerant structure that can hold both P and ¬P with an Active Conflict marker while remaining usable, with Zero/Lord/Sārathi each playing their established roles around the conflict.

anchor: DDD interpretation ... KnowledgeState ... Assertion ... Evidence ... Conflict ... Resolution ... KnowledgeEvent ... EvidenceAcquired, AssertionIntroduced, AssertionCorroborated, AssertionQualified, ConflictDetected, ConflictResolved, AssertionRetracted, AssertionSuperseded, AssertionExpired
statement: Introduces six DDD concepts (KnowledgeState, Assertion, Evidence, Conflict, Resolution, KnowledgeEvent) with nine named domain events (EvidenceAcquired, AssertionIntroduced, AssertionCorroborated, AssertionQualified, ConflictDetected, ConflictResolved, AssertionRetracted, AssertionSuperseded, AssertionExpired).

anchor: Aggregate boundary ... I would not make the entire KnowledgeOS one giant KnowledgeState aggregate. Instead, conceptually: Knowledge / Assertion / Evidence / EvidenceRelation / Conflict / Resolution / KnowledgeEvent with bounded contexts governing different invariants. This prevents the kernel becomi
statement: Rejects a single monolithic KnowledgeState aggregate in favor of separate bounded-context aggregates (Assertion, Evidence, EvidenceRelation, Conflict, Resolution, KnowledgeEvent), preventing a 'god aggregate'.

anchor: A critical mathematical distinction: update vs recomputation ... Incremental update K_{t+1}=\delta(K_t,e_t) ... Full recomputation K_t=F(K_0,H_t) ... IncrementalState must be reconstructible from history. This is an excellent deterministic assurance mechanism. ... Verification invariant ... Incremen
statement: States that both incremental update (K_{t+1}=δ(K_t,e_t)) and full historical recomputation (K_t=F(K_0,H_t)) must be supported and must agree — Incremental(K_0,H_t)=Reconstruct(K_0,H_t) under the same policy/ontology versions — as a testable drift-detection invariant.

anchor: A concrete example ... K_0=\emptyset ... Event 1 API observation e_1:P ... Event 2 Filesystem observation e_2:P independent ... Event 3 Old document e_3:P' Context(P')=2024 ... no current conflict ... Event 4 Current production inventory e_4: NexusVersion=3.70 ... C_1=(A_1,A_2,VersionEqualityRule,Co
statement: Works a four-event Nexus-version example from K_0=∅ through API observation, independent filesystem corroboration, a contextually-scoped 2024 document (no conflict), and a current production inventory reading that finally creates an explicit Conflict object C_1 rather than silently replacing an assertion.

anchor: What happens if a conflict is resolved? ... 3.69 = staging, 3.70 = production ... P_1: Nexus(staging)=3.69, P_2: Nexus(production)=3.70. The conflict disappears because the propositions were insufficiently contextualized. Conflict may reveal a missing dimension. That connects directly back to the Id
statement: Shows a conflict resolving by discovering a missing context dimension (staging vs production), establishing that Conflict may reveal a missing dimension, connecting back to the Ideal State and Zero.

anchor: New evidence can therefore reduce one discrepancy while creating another ... Conflict=0. But discovers EnvironmentDimension=Unknown. Then \Delta_{conflict}\downarrow while \Delta_{dimension}\uparrow. This is why KnowledgeOS cannot optimize only one metric. Knowledge evolution is multidimensional.
statement: Argues knowledge evolution is inherently multidimensional: resolving one discrepancy (Conflict→0) can create another (a newly discovered Unknown dimension), so KnowledgeOS cannot optimize a single scalar metric.

anchor: Formal transition model ... K_{t+1} = \delta_\rho(K_t,a_t,e_t) ... H_{t+1}=H_t\Vert Event_t ... Event_t=(Action,EvidenceAssessment,StateDelta,Provenance,PolicyVersion) ... The complete epistemic cycle ... K_t\rightarrow Zero\rightarrow \Delta_t\rightarrow Lord\rightarrow CandidateAction\rightarrow S
statement: Consolidates the formal transition model K_{t+1}=δ_ρ(K_t,a_t,e_t) with history append H_{t+1}=H_t‖Event_t where Event_t=(Action,EvidenceAssessment,StateDelta,Provenance,PolicyVersion), assembling the complete cycle K_t→Zero→Δ_t→Lord→CandidateAction→Sārathi→Acquisition→Evidence→Assessment→Conclusion→K_{t+1}.

anchor: The strongest invariants established in Step 7 ... K1 — Evidence does not directly become knowledge ... K2 — History is preserved ... K3 — Contradiction is representable ... K4 — Temporal distinction ... K5 — Reconstructibility ... K6 — Policy versioning ... K7 — Semantic versioning ... K8 — State t
statement: Consolidates eight named invariants K1-K8: Evidence⇏AcceptedKnowledge, Superseded/Retracted≠Deleted, P and ¬P representable without collapse, SourceTime≠AcquisitionTime≠ValidityTime, K_t=Reconstruct(K_0,H_t), policy versioning, semantic versioning, and multidimensional (non-single-lifecycle) state transition Σ_{t+1}=ε(Σ_t,o_t).

anchor: One thing remains deliberately unresolved ... When exactly is a conclusion allowed to modify the Knowledge State? ... Must be independently corroborated ... One authoritative source is sufficient ... Human approval required ... Probability ≥ 0.95. These are not universal mathematics. They are govern
statement: Explicitly leaves unresolved when a Conclusion may modify the Knowledge State, listing four candidate acceptance policies (independent corroboration required / single authoritative source / human approval / probability threshold) as governance decisions that must not be buried inside δ.

anchor: Step 7 verdict ... STRUCTURALLY RESOLVED but with one remaining policy boundary: AcceptancePolicy must be explicitly defined before implementation. K_{t+1} = \delta_\rho(K_t,Conclusion_t) with Conclusion_t=g_\rho(EvidenceAssessment_t,IdealState_t,Context_t).
statement: Declares Step 7 structurally resolved modulo the still-undefined AcceptancePolicy, consolidating K_{t+1}=δ_ρ(K_t,Conclusion_t) with Conclusion_t=g_ρ(EvidenceAssessment_t,IdealState_t,Context_t).

anchor:
Step 8 — the next question ... When is an assessed proposition admitted into the Knowledge State, and when must it remain merely supported, proposed, contested, or unresolved? ... Step 8 — Epistemic Acceptance and Commitment ... Supported 
eq Accepted 
eq Committed 
eq True ... acceptance is wher
statement: Poses Step 8's question of when an assessed proposition is admitted into the Knowledge State versus remaining Supported/Proposed/Contested/Unresolved, previewing the distinction Supported≠Accepted≠Committed≠True and framing acceptance as where epistemology meets governance.

lineage_claims.quote: Step 8 -- Epistemic Acceptance and Commitment

anchor:
The central distinction is: Supported 
eq Accepted 
eq Committed 
eq True. This distinction should become one of the core laws of KnowledgeOS.
statement: States the governing distinction of Step 8 as a candidate core law of KnowledgeOS: Supported ≠ Accepted ≠ Committed ≠ True.

anchor: The problem ... Strong supporting evidence, No known contradiction, Current, High provenance quality ... Can KnowledgeOS now put P into the Knowledge State as accepted knowledge? Not necessarily. There is a missing concept: AcceptancePolicy. The evidence tells us what the evidence supports. The acce
statement: Argues even strong, uncontradicted, current, high-provenance evidence does not automatically warrant acceptance, introducing AcceptancePolicy as the missing concept determining what may be admitted as accepted knowledge.

anchor: Four epistemic statuses ... Candidate \rightarrow Supported \rightarrow Accepted \rightarrow Committed ... Supported \rightarrow Contested ... Supported \rightarrow Rejected ... Candidate \rightarrow Unresolved ... These are not simply levels of "confidence." They represent different domain states.
statement: Distinguishes Candidate/Supported/Accepted/Committed as a branching progression (not a confidence scale), with additional branches to Contested, Rejected, and Unresolved, insisting these are distinct domain states.

anchor: Candidate ... A proposition becomes a candidate when KnowledgeOS has reason to represent it but does not yet have sufficient basis to accept it. ... LLM extracted from document ... Candidate(P)=True but Accepted(P)=False. This is particularly important for AI-generated knowledge.
statement: Defines Candidate(P) status (proposition represented but not yet accepted), illustrated by an LLM-extracted proposition, flagged as particularly important for AI-generated knowledge.

anchor: Supported ... Supported_\rho(P) = Assessment_\rho(P)\models SupportCondition_\rho ... The evidence provides a defensible basis for the proposition under the selected assessment policy. But Supported(P)\not\Rightarrow Accepted(P).
statement: Defines Supported_ρ(P) as Assessment_ρ(P) satisfying a policy-specific SupportCondition_ρ, explicitly not implying Accepted(P).

anchor: Accepted ... Accept_\rho(P,EA) \rightarrow AcceptedAssertion subject to the acceptance policy. ... One authoritative current source is sufficient ... Two independent observations ... Accepted_{\rho_1}(P)=True while Accepted_{\rho_2}(P)=False. This is not a mathematical contradiction. It is policy de
statement: Defines Accept_ρ(P,EA)→AcceptedAssertion as policy-relative, showing the same evidence can be Accepted under one policy (single authoritative source) and not under another (requiring two independent observations) — policy dependence, not contradiction.

anchor: Commitment ... an organization may accept ... but still not be committed to using that assertion as a basis for an operational decision. "We accept that Nexus is 3.69, but migration approval requires an additional infrastructure verification." Accepted(P)\not\Rightarrow Committed(P). Commitment mean
statement: Defines Commitment as distinct from Acceptance: Accepted(P) ⇏ Committed(P), illustrated by an organization accepting a fact but still requiring additional verification before migration approval; commitment means willingness to rely on the proposition for a defined purpose/action.

anchor: Commitment is purpose-dependent ... Commit_\rho(P,Purpose,Authority) ... Commit(P,migration,ArchitectureBoard) may require more than Commit(P,internal research,Engineer). Commit(P,P_1)\neq Commit(P,P_2). This fits our earlier Ideal State principle: I_t(P_1)\neq I_t(P_2).
statement: Defines Commit_ρ(P,Purpose,Authority) as purpose-dependent, e.g. migration commitment requiring Architecture Board authority versus lighter requirements for internal research, echoing the earlier purpose-dependence of the Ideal State.

anchor: Truth remains outside the state machine ... Accepted(P)\neq True(P) and Committed(P)\neq True(P). KnowledgeOS does not have an oracle for reality. It records what is currently supported, accepted, and/or committed under a defined epistemic and governance regime.
statement: States that neither Accepted(P) nor Committed(P) equals True(P): KnowledgeOS has no oracle for reality, only records what is supported/accepted/committed under a defined regime.

anchor: Formal acceptance function ... \alpha_\rho: EA\times P\times C \rightarrow \mathcal S_A ... \mathcal S_A=\{Candidate,Supported,Accepted,Rejected,Contested,Unresolved\} ... an assertion can be Supported + Contested. So again, we should be careful about a single enum.
statement: Defines α_ρ:EA×P×C→S_A over six statuses, warning against treating S_A as a single mutually-exclusive enum since e.g. Supported+Contested can co-occur.

anchor: Better: acceptance as a multidimensional status ... \Omega_A=(SupportStatus,AcceptanceStatus,CommitmentStatus,ContestStatus) ... Support: Strong, Acceptance: Accepted, Commitment: Committed, Contest: Active. This looks strange initially, but it accurately represents real organizational knowledge.
statement: Defines acceptance status as a four-dimensional vector Ω_A=(SupportStatus,AcceptanceStatus,CommitmentStatus,ContestStatus), with a worked example showing Accepted+Committed+Contest:Active as coherent, accurately reflecting real organizational knowledge.

anchor: Why "Accepted + Contested" is possible ... an architecture board has formally accepted ... another architect disputes ... Accepted(P)=True while Contested(P)=True. This is not logically impossible. ... The proposition is institutionally accepted while still being epistemically contested. This is exa
statement: Justifies Accepted+Contested coexisting via an architecture-board example (formally accepted decision still disputed by an architect), establishing that epistemic status and governance status must not be collapsed.

anchor: Acceptance policy ... \rho_A = AcceptancePolicy ... Evidence requirements N_{independent}\geq2 ... Source requirements Authority(Source)\geq A_{min} ... Temporal requirements Age(e)\leq T_{max} ... Conflict requirements ActiveConflict(P)=False ... Human approval ... Statistical threshold Pr(P\mid E)
statement: Defines AcceptancePolicy ρ_A as specifying six example condition types (independent-evidence count, source authority minimum, evidence-age maximum, no active conflict, human approval, statistical threshold) — explicitly examples of policy, not universal law.

anchor: This gives us a clean separation ... Mathematics defines what the evidence assessment means. Policy defines when an assessment is sufficient for acceptance. Governance defines who has authority to commit to that knowledge. Assessment \rightarrow AcceptancePolicy \rightarrow Acceptance \rightarrow Go
statement: Draws a three-way separation — mathematics (what assessment means), policy (when acceptance is sufficient), governance (who may commit) — formalized as Assessment→AcceptancePolicy→Acceptance→Governance→Commitment.

anchor: DDD interpretation ... a bounded context around Knowledge Commitment. Assertion ... EvidenceAssessment ... AcceptancePolicy ... AcceptanceDecision ... Commitment ... Authority ... These should not be hidden inside the Assertion entity.
statement: Proposes a Knowledge Commitment bounded context with six concepts (Assertion, EvidenceAssessment, AcceptancePolicy, AcceptanceDecision, Commitment, Authority) that must not be hidden inside the Assertion entity.

anchor: Acceptance is a domain event ... AssertionAccepted should be emitted. AssertionId, AssessmentId, PolicyId, PolicyVersion, Authority, Context, EffectiveFrom, DecisionBasis, Timestamp. This creates an auditable transition.
statement: Defines an AssertionAccepted domain event carrying AssertionId, AssessmentId, PolicyId/Version, Authority, Context, EffectiveFrom, DecisionBasis, Timestamp for auditability.

anchor: Rejection is different from absence of acceptance ... NotAccepted\neq Rejected ... Evidence: insufficient ... The correct state may be Unresolved. It does not mean P=False. Unresolved\neq Rejected. This is critical for incomplete real-world knowledge.
statement: States NotAccepted≠Rejected and Unresolved≠Rejected: insufficient evidence should yield Unresolved, not a claim that P is false — critical for incomplete real-world knowledge.

anchor: Example ... Production Nexus is backed up. ... Infrastructure engineer says yes ... Backup configuration not inspected ... No restore test ... Support: Moderate, Uncertainty: High, Verification: Insufficient ... KnowledgeOS should not conclude \neg P. Nor Accepted(P). The correct result may be Unres
statement: Works a backup-verification example where weak/unverified evidence (engineer's verbal yes, uninspected config, no restore test) correctly yields Unresolved(P) with a Lord recommendation to verify configuration and run a restore test, rather than either Accepted(P) or ¬P.

anchor: Acceptance and Ideal State ... MustBeVerified(BackupStatus) ... Supported(P) may still fail the ideal requirement: \Sigma_K(P)\not\models I^K(P). Accepted(P) \not\Rightarrow IdealSatisfied(P). A proposition can be accepted while the knowledge objective remains incomplete.
statement: Connects Acceptance to the Ideal State: Accepted(P) ⇏ IdealSatisfied(P) — a proposition can be accepted while the underlying knowledge objective (e.g. independent verification) remains incomplete.

anchor: Example ... Nexus = 3.69 Accepted. But the Ideal State requires MustBeKnown, MustBeCurrent, MustBeIndependentlyVerified ... Independent verification = no ... Accepted(P)=True but \Delta_t\neq\emptyset. Acceptance does not mean completion.
statement: Worked example: an accepted Nexus-version assertion still leaves a nonempty discrepancy Δ_t because independent verification is missing — 'Acceptance does not mean completion.'

anchor: This protects us from a major design mistake ... LLM found answer ↓ Answer accepted ↓ Gap closed. Our model rejects that shortcut. Instead: LLM found candidate ↓ Evidence assessment ↓ Acceptance policy ↓ Accepted? ↓ Ideal-state evaluation ↓ Gap closed? These are separate decisions.
statement: Warns against the shortcut 'LLM found answer → gap closed', mandating the full separated pipeline (candidate → assessment → acceptance policy → accepted? → ideal-state evaluation → gap closed?) as distinct decisions.

anchor: Commitment introduces authority ... Committed(P,Migration) may require Authority=ArchitectureBoard. Authority is part of commitment, not evidence. A manager's authority does not make evidence more truthful. It determines what the organization is permitted to commit to.
statement: States Authority is part of commitment, not evidence: an authority figure's approval does not make evidence more truthful, it only determines what the organization is permitted to commit to.

anchor: Human versus AI ... An LLM may produce Candidate(P) ... even Supported(P) if its output is appropriately assessed. But LLMOutput\not\Rightarrow OrganizationalCommitment. A human or governed process may be required. This is an extremely important KnowledgeOS safety property.
statement: States LLMOutput ⇏ OrganizationalCommitment as a KnowledgeOS safety property: an LLM can produce Candidate or even Supported status, but organizational commitment requires a human or governed process.

anchor: Formal state transition ... (EA,P,\rho_A) \rightarrow AcceptanceOutcome ... (AcceptanceOutcome,Authority,Purpose) \rightarrow CommitmentOutcome ... Evidence \rightarrow Assessment \rightarrow Acceptance \rightarrow Commitment is formally distinct.
statement: Formalizes (EvidenceAssessment,P,ρ_A)→AcceptanceOutcome and (AcceptanceOutcome,Authority,Purpose)→CommitmentOutcome as two distinct formal transitions.

anchor: Knowledge State integration ... K_t \xrightarrow{AssertionAccepted} K_{t+1} ... K_{t+1} \xrightarrow{CommitmentEstablished} K_{t+2}. But the underlying assertion does not change truth value. Its institutional status changes.
statement: Models acceptance and commitment as two successive Knowledge State transitions (via AssertionAccepted then CommitmentEstablished events) that change institutional status, never the assertion's truth value.

anchor: A useful formal decomposition ... A=(P,\Sigma,\Omega,\Pi,\tau,Ctx) ... \Sigma=(Acquisition,Support,Uncertainty,Validity) ... \Omega=(SupportStatus,AcceptanceStatus,CommitmentStatus,ContestStatus). Epistemic state ... Governance state ... That separation is extremely important.
statement: Decomposes an assertion as A=(P,Σ,Ω,Π,τ,Ctx) combining the Step-7 epistemic state Σ (Acquisition,Support,Uncertainty,Validity) with the new governance state Ω (SupportStatus,AcceptanceStatus,CommitmentStatus,ContestStatus), keeping epistemic and governance dimensions separate.

anchor: The acceptance lattice question ... Candidate, Supported, Accepted, Committed look like a ladder, but they are not universally ordered. Accepted\not\Rightarrow Committed. Contested can coexist with Accepted. AcceptanceStatus should be modeled as a state space, not a scalar hierarchy.
statement: Corrects the apparent ladder Candidate→Supported→Accepted→Committed: it is not a universal ordering (Accepted⇏Committed; Contested can coexist with Accepted), so AcceptanceStatus must be a state space, not a scalar hierarchy.

anchor: Mathematical structure ... \mathcal O=\mathcal O_S\times\mathcal O_A\times\mathcal O_C\times\mathcal O_X ... \Omega_A\in\mathcal O ... \omega: \Omega_A\times Event\times Policy \rightharpoonup \Omega_A
statement: Formalizes the acceptance-status space as a product O=O_S×O_A×O_C×O_X (support/acceptance/commitment/contest statuses) with Ω_A∈O and a partial transition function ω:Ω_A×Event×Policy⇀Ω_A.

anchor:
The most important invariants ... A1 Supported
ot\Rightarrow Accepted ... A2 Accepted
ot\Rightarrow Committed ... A3 Accepted
ot\Rightarrow Truth ... A4 Unresolved
ot\Rightarrow Rejected ... A5 NotAccepted
ot\Rightarrow False ... A6 Authority determines commitment, not evidential truth ... A7 A
statement: Adds ten candidate constitutional invariants A1-A10 to the KnowledgeOS epistemic constitution, covering Supported/Accepted/Committed/Truth/Unresolved/NotAccepted non-implications, authority-vs-truth, policy governance of acceptance, purpose/context governance of commitment, auditability of historical acceptance, and acceptance not implying ideal-state satisfaction.

anchor: The full KnowledgeOS epistemic pipeline ... Evidence → Evidence Relations → Evidence Assessment → Acceptance Policy → Accepted/Rejected/Unresolved → Authority/Purpose → Commitment → Knowledge State → Ideal State → Discrepancy → Next Acquisition. And the cycle repeats.
statement: Assembles the full epistemic pipeline: Evidence→Relations→Assessment→AcceptancePolicy→{Accepted,Rejected,Unresolved}→Authority/Purpose→Commitment→KnowledgeState→IdealState→Discrepancy→NextAcquisition, cycling back.

anchor: Step 8 verdict ... STRUCTURALLY RESOLVED ... a rigorous distinction between Evidence, Assessment, Support, Acceptance, Commitment, Truth. These should never be collapsed.
statement: Declares Step 8 structurally resolved, having established a rigorous six-way distinction (Evidence/Assessment/Support/Acceptance/Commitment/Truth) that must never be collapsed.

anchor: Step 9 — The next problem ... How does KnowledgeOS represent multiple competing conclusions about the same proposition, and how does it reason when the Knowledge State is intentionally inconsistent? ... P\land\neg P must not cause the entire knowledge base to explode. ... Contradiction, Paraconsiste
statement: Poses Step 9: formalize Contradiction, Paraconsistency, and Belief Revision, with seven required capabilities for handling P,¬P∈K_t (represent both, determine genuine conflict, prevent logical explosion, contextualize applicability, decide supersession, preserve historically, identify resolving evidence).

lineage_claims.quote: Contradiction, Paraconsistency, and Belief Revision

anchor: The fundamental problem ... P\land\neg P ... principle of explosion ... P,\neg P\vdash Q for arbitrary Q, the Knowledge State becomes useless. KnowledgeOS must tolerate contradiction without logical explosion.
statement: Requires KnowledgeOS tolerate contradiction (P∧¬P) without classical logical explosion (P,¬P⊢Q for arbitrary Q), since explosion would make the Knowledge State useless.

anchor: First distinction: contradiction versus inconsistency ... Contradiction ... Conflict(A_1,A_2,Ctx)=True. Inconsistency ... a set of assertions that cannot all simultaneously satisfy a specified logical model. Contradiction is relational. Inconsistency is a property of a set/state.
statement: Distinguishes Contradiction (a relational property between two specific assertions under a context) from Inconsistency (a property of an entire assertion set/state under a logical model).

anchor: Context must be checked first ... Nexus_{Production}=3.70 and Nexus_{Staging}=3.69 ... no contradiction because Context(P_1)\neq Context(P_2). Different context \Rightarrow not necessarily contradictory. Many apparent contradictions are actually missing-dimension problems.
statement: Reaffirms that differing contexts (production vs staging) can make apparently conflicting values non-contradictory, restating that many apparent contradictions are missing-dimension problems.

anchor: Contradiction requires a conflict rule ... Conflict_\rho(A_i,A_j) = Rule_\rho(P_i,P_j,C_i,C_j) ... Version(x)=v_1 \land Version(x)=v_2 \land v_1\neq v_2 is contradictory if the two assertions refer to the same system; same environment; same temporal scope. Without those conditions: DifferentValues\n
statement: Defines Conflict_ρ(A_i,A_j)=Rule_ρ(P_i,P_j,C_i,C_j): contradiction requires an explicit rule checking same system/environment/temporal scope, so DifferentValues ≠ Contradiction without those conditions.

anchor: Conflict graph ... a knowledge conflict graph: G_C=(A,L_C) ... A1: Nexus production = 3.69 conflict A2: Nexus production = 3.70. The conflict is explicitly represented. Neither assertion has to be deleted.
statement: Defines a knowledge conflict graph G_C=(A,L_C) (assertions and conflict relations) representing conflicts explicitly without deleting either assertion.

anchor: KnowledgeOS should preserve both assertions ... A_1\in K_t \land A_2\in K_t \land Conflict(A_1,A_2)=Active. This is a legitimate Knowledge State. The state is inconsistent with respect to that proposition, but it is not computationally unusable.
statement: States that a Knowledge State holding both A1 and A2 with an Active conflict marker is legitimate and computationally usable, despite being inconsistent with respect to that proposition.

anchor: Paraconsistent principle ... P,\neg P \not\Rightarrow Q for arbitrary Q. Contradiction must remain local. ... we do not necessarily need to commit the entire KnowledgeOS kernel to one particular paraconsistent logic ... the kernel must support the invariant: Local inconsistency does not imply global
statement: States the paraconsistent principle P,¬P ⇏ Q (contradiction must remain local), without committing the kernel to any specific paraconsistent logic (e.g. Priest's LP), requiring only that local inconsistency not imply global triviality.

anchor: A useful four-valued interpretation ... P supported ... \neg P supported ... Unknown ... Supported true-side ... Supported false-side ... Conflicted ... \mathbb B=\{00,10,01,11\} ... This is much more expressive than True/False.
statement: Defines a four-valued epistemic-status model B={00,10,01,11} (Unknown, P-supported, ¬P-supported, Conflicted) as more expressive than binary True/False.

anchor: Important correction ... We should not interpret 10=True and 01=False. They mean: Evidence currently supports one side. This is epistemic status, not metaphysical truth. Four-valued epistemic status\neq Four-valued truth.
statement: Corrects a likely misreading of the four-valued model: its values denote epistemic support status, not metaphysical truth values — Four-valued epistemic status ≠ Four-valued truth.

anchor: This fits our existing epistemic model ... \Sigma_A=(Acquisition,Support,Uncertainty,Validity) and conflict remains external: C=(A_i,A_j,Rule,Context,Status). \Sigma_A does not need to contain Conflicted because conflict belongs to the relationship between assertions.
statement: Confirms conflict is a relational property external to the per-assertion state Σ_A, which need not include a 'Conflicted' field since conflict belongs between assertions, not within one.

anchor: Conflict intensity is not a universal scalar ... ConflictScore=0.8 ... I recommend we don't. Instead represent Conflict: Assertions, Rule, Context, EvidenceBasis, Status: Active. Conflict representation is fundamental. Conflict score is derived.
statement: Warns against a scalar ConflictScore, preferring a structured conflict record (assertions, rule, context, evidence basis, status): conflict representation is fundamental, any scalar score is derived.

anchor: Belief revision ... K_t\models P and new evidence supports \neg P. K_{t+1}=Revise(K_t,e). Revision does not necessarily mean deleting P. retain both and mark conflict; contextualize; downgrade one; retract one; supersede one; accept one and reject the other; leave unresolved. Which occurs depends on
statement: Defines the revision operation K_{t+1}=Revise(K_t,e) with seven possible policy-dependent outcomes (retain both with conflict marked, contextualize, downgrade, retract, supersede, accept-one-reject-other, leave unresolved) — none of which is automatic deletion.

anchor: AGM-style belief revision is useful—but not sufficient ... revision; contraction; consistency; minimal change. But KnowledgeOS has a different requirement: We may intentionally retain inconsistent information. Therefore classical consistency-preserving belief revision is not sufficient as the sole k
statement: Argues classical AGM-style (consistency-preserving) belief revision is insufficient alone, since KnowledgeOS may intentionally retain inconsistent information; needs a more general evidence-based, contradiction-tolerant revision model.

anchor: Three different responses to conflict ... A. Contextual resolution ... No real contradiction. B. Epistemic resolution ... one assertion may become Retracted or Rejected. C. Irreducible conflict ... Conflict=Unresolved and KnowledgeOS retains both. This is a perfectly legitimate endpoint.
statement: Classifies three conflict responses: Contextual resolution (no real contradiction once context is added), Epistemic resolution (one side retracted/rejected on evidential grounds), and Irreducible conflict (both retained as Unresolved, a legitimate endpoint).

anchor: Unresolvable is not failure ... two authoritative sources disagree and there is no way to determine which is correct. KnowledgeOS should be able to say P: Contested rather than inventing P=True. Unresolvable is a valid knowledge state.
statement: States Unresolvable is a valid knowledge state: when two authoritative sources irreconcilably disagree, KnowledgeOS should record P:Contested rather than inventing a resolution.

anchor: What should Zero do? ... Zero detects Conflict(A_1,A_2). It creates a discrepancy d_{conflict} with involved assertions; conflict rule; context; severity; evidence basis; age; impact. Zero(K,I) \rightarrow \Delta_{conflict}.
statement: Extends Zero's role to conflict detection: Zero(K,I)→Δ_conflict, a structured discrepancy record with assertions, rule, context, severity, evidence basis, age, impact.

anchor: What should Lord do? ... What information could resolve this conflict? ... Query live API. Inspect deployment manifest. Inspect filesystem. Ask system owner. The candidates are evaluated using Step 6: VOE(q). Conflict \rightarrow Gap \rightarrow CandidateEvidence \rightarrow ExpectedDiscrepancyReduc
statement: Extends Lord's role to conflict resolution: proposing candidate evidence acquisitions (query API, inspect manifest/filesystem, ask owner) evaluated via the Step 6 Value-of-Evidence machinery, connecting Conflict→Gap→CandidateEvidence→ExpectedDiscrepancyReduction.

anchor: What should Sārathi do? ... severity; purpose; cost; authority; safety; urgency; expected value. It may decide Investigate. Or AcceptRisk. Or Defer. Or CommitWithConflict. A decision does not necessarily require complete epistemic resolution.
statement: Extends Sārathi's role to conflict handling with four possible decisions (Investigate/AcceptRisk/Defer/CommitWithConflict), noting a decision does not require complete epistemic resolution.

anchor: Example — Architecture decision ... Migration is technically feasible ... Migration introduces unacceptable operational risk ... TechnicalFeasibility=True ... OperationalRisk=High ... the apparent conflict becomes a multi-dimensional decision problem. Conflict detection can reveal a modeling deficie
statement: Shows an apparent architecture-decision contradiction (feasible vs unacceptable risk) resolves into a multi-dimensional decision problem once separated into distinct dimensions (TechnicalFeasibility, OperationalRisk) — conflict detection can reveal a modeling deficiency.

anchor: Temporal conflict ... Nexus=3.69 at t_1=2024 and Nexus=3.85 at t_2=2026. There is no contradiction if t_1\neq t_2. Temporal context must be part of conflict detection. This is one of the reasons we separated SourceTime, AcquisitionTime, ValidityTime.
statement: Requires temporal context be part of conflict detection, since two differently-timed version assertions are not contradictory — reaffirming the earlier SourceTime/AcquisitionTime/ValidityTime separation.

anchor: Supersession ... P_{old} \rightarrow P_{new} we should represent Supersedes(P_{new},P_{old}) rather than Conflict(P_{old},P_{new}). Nexus 3.69 superseded by Nexus 3.85. The old assertion remains historically valid for its period.
statement: Distinguishes Supersession (Supersedes(P_new,P_old), old assertion remains historically valid) from Conflict, for cases where the domain has genuinely changed over time rather than truly disagreeing.

anchor: Belief revision operations ... \mathcal R_K=\{Contextualize,Corroborate,Downgrade,Retract,Supersede,Accept,Reject,Defer,Resolve\} ... Revise: K\times\mathcal R_K \rightharpoonup K. Again, the operation is partial and policy governed.
statement: Defines a nine-operation belief-revision set R_K (Contextualize/Corroborate/Downgrade/Retract/Supersede/Accept/Reject/Defer/Resolve) with Revise:K×R_K⇀K as a partial, policy-governed function.

anchor: Revision should minimize unnecessary change ... change as little as necessary. MinimalRevision should be preferred where the policy permits. ... K_{t+1} = K_t \oplus \Delta_{necessary}. Local evidence change \Rightarrow local knowledge revision unless dependencies propagate the change.
statement: Adopts a MinimalRevision principle from belief-revision theory: change only what is necessary (K_{t+1}=K_t⊕Δ_necessary), so local evidence change implies local knowledge revision unless dependencies propagate it.

anchor: But dependencies can propagate revision ... A\rightarrow B where B=Infer(A). If A is retracted, B may become unsupported. Retract(A) \rightarrow Reassess(B). This is why the provenance graph is not merely an audit feature. It is part of the semantic dependency model.
statement: Argues retraction can propagate through dependency (Retract(A)→Reassess(B) when B was inferred from A), making the provenance graph part of the semantic dependency model, not merely an audit feature.

anchor: Important: not every dependency means automatic retraction ... B was derived partly from A_1 and A_2. If A_1 is retracted, B may still remain supported by A_2. Dependency propagation means reassessment, not automatic deletion.
statement: States dependency propagation means reassessment, not automatic deletion — a conclusion derived from multiple sources may survive the retraction of one.

anchor: Formal revision function ... K_{t+1} = Revise_\rho(K_t,e_t,EA_t) ... identify affected assertions; recalculate assessments; update conflict relations; update acceptance status; propagate to dependent assertions; preserve history.
statement: Consolidates the revision function K_{t+1}=Revise_ρ(K_t,e_t,EA_t) into six steps: identify affected assertions, recalculate assessments, update conflict relations, update acceptance status, propagate to dependents, preserve history.

anchor: Computational viability ... For finite knowledge graphs, yes. G_K=(V,E) is finite for any finite current state. A new event affects a reachable subgraph: Reachable(e,G_K). We can recompute the affected region rather than the entire Knowledge State. ... provided the inference and semantic comparison
statement: Argues revision is computationally tractable for finite knowledge graphs by recomputing only the reachable affected subgraph Reachable(e,G_K), conditional on the inference/semantic-comparison policies themselves being computationally bounded.

anchor: But there is a theoretical boundary ... General logical entailment can be undecidable ... Semantic equivalence of arbitrary natural-language propositions is not generally decidable. Kernel decidability from Open world semantic inference. The kernel can guarantee deterministic handling of explicit re
statement: States a theoretical boundary: general logical entailment and natural-language semantic equivalence are not generally decidable, so Kernel decidability must be kept separate from Open-world semantic inference, the latter marked Status=Inferred/Proposed until accepted.

anchor: This is a major KnowledgeOS principle ... Undecidable semantic questions must never be silently converted into deterministic facts. Deterministic: Provenance = D. AI inference: A probably means P. Assessment: semantic equivalence = Inferred. Human/policy: Accepted. This gives us a clean epistemic bo
statement: States the principle that undecidable semantic questions must never be silently converted into deterministic facts, illustrated by a four-stage pipeline (deterministic provenance → AI inference → Inferred assessment → human/policy acceptance) as a clean computation/interpretation boundary.

anchor: Step 9 formal model ... K_t=(A_t,E_t,R_t,C_t,H_t,\Gamma_t) with C_t\subseteq A_t\times A_t. A conflict exists when Conflict_\rho(A_i,A_j,Ctx)=True. Revision: K_{t+1}=Revise_\rho(K_t,e_t). and crucially P,\neg P\in K_t \not\Rightarrow Q\in K_t for arbitrary Q.
statement: Consolidates the Step 9 formal model: K_t with conflicts C_t⊆A_t×A_t, conflict predicate Conflict_ρ(A_i,A_j,Ctx), revision K_{t+1}=Revise_ρ(K_t,e_t), and the crucial non-explosion guarantee P,¬P∈K_t ⇏ Q∈K_t.

anchor: Step 9 invariants ... C1 — Local contradiction ... C2 — No explosion ... C3 — Contextual conflict ... C4 — Temporal distinction ... C5 — Supersession preservation ... C6 — Revision preservation ... C7 — Dependency propagation ... C8 — Unresolvable conflict is valid
statement: States eight candidate invariants C1-C8: conflict is local, no explosion (P,¬P⇏Q), conflict requires compatible context, temporal change ≠ contradiction, superseded ≠ deleted, revision preserves historical provenance, retraction propagates as reassessment not automatic deletion, and unresolvable conflict ≠ system failure.

anchor: Where we are now ... Evidence \rightarrow EvidenceRelations \rightarrow Assessment \rightarrow Acceptance \rightarrow KnowledgeState \rightarrow Conflict/Gap \rightarrow Revision \rightarrow NewKnowledgeState ... K_t \rightarrow Zero \rightarrow Lord \rightarrow Sārathi \rightarrow Acquisition \righ
statement: Assembles the extended pipeline (Evidence→EvidenceRelations→Assessment→Acceptance→KnowledgeState→Conflict/Gap→Revision→NewKnowledgeState) alongside the active Zero→Lord→Sārathi→Acquisition→K_{t+1} loop, declared a coherent computational architecture.

anchor: Step 9 verdict ... STRUCTURALLY RESOLVED with one deliberate limitation: We have not selected a particular paraconsistent logic/calculus as the universal reasoning engine. I recommend not doing so yet. The kernel should guarantee Contradiction tolerance + No explosion + Explicit conflict + Revision
statement: Declares Step 9 structurally resolved while deliberately not selecting any specific paraconsistent logic, requiring only that the kernel guarantee contradiction tolerance, no explosion, explicit conflict representation, and revision, leaving specific reasoning engines pluggable.

anchor: Step 10 — Next question ... How does KnowledgeOS determine whether an assertion follows logically from other accepted assertions? ... A_1,A_2,\ldots,A_n \vdash_\rho A_{n+1} ... observation; extraction; deduction; induction; abduction; calculation; analogy; LLM inference; human interpretation. ... wh
statement: Poses Step 10: formalize policy-relative entailment A1,...,An⊢_ρ A_{n+1} across nine inference modes (observation, extraction, deduction, induction, abduction, calculation, analogy, LLM inference, human interpretation), determining what is deterministic vs statistical/AI, and how derived assertions inherit provenance/uncertainty.

lineage_claims.quote: Step 10 -- Inference and Derivation

anchor: A common mistake is to say A_1,A_2\Rightarrow A_3 therefore A_3 has "the same confidence" as A_1,A_2. That is generally false. The epistemic quality of a derived proposition depends on what kind of inference produced it, what premises it depends on, how those premises depend on one another, and what
statement: Warns against assuming a derived proposition inherits its premises' confidence wholesale; its epistemic quality depends on the inference kind, premise dependencies, and the inference rule's own uncertainty.

anchor: The fundamental problem ... A_1=Strong and A_2=Weak. A_3=A_1\land A_2 ... It cannot simply inherit Strong. Nor should we arbitrarily assign Weak. ... \Sigma_{derived} = Propagate_\rho(\Sigma_{premises},Rule,Method,Dependency,Context)
statement: Defines Σ_derived=Propagate_ρ(Σ_premises,Rule,Method,Dependency,Context) as the general propagation function, illustrated by a conjunction of a Strong and a Weak premise where neither naive inheritance is correct.

anchor: First distinction: uncertainty has different origins ... Premise uncertainty U_{premise} ... Inference uncertainty U_{inference} ... Model uncertainty U_{model} ... Measurement uncertainty U_{measurement} ... Semantic uncertainty U_{semantic} ... Context uncertainty U_{context} ... Uncertainty\neq o
statement: Enumerates six distinct uncertainty origins — premise, inference, model, measurement, semantic, context — establishing Uncertainty ≠ one universal quantity.

anchor: This confirms our multidimensional model ... U_A=(U_{source},U_{measurement},U_{semantic},U_{inference},U_{model},U_{context}) ... more rigorous than U_A=0.3. A scalar may later be derived if a policy needs one.
statement: Defines a six-dimension uncertainty vector U_A, more rigorous than a bare scalar U_A=0.3, from which a policy-specific scalar may later be derived.

anchor: Dependency graph ... G_D=(V,E_D) ... A1, A2 → A3 → A5 ... Deps(A_3)=\{A_1,A_2\} and Deps(A_5)=\{A_3\}. Therefore uncertainty can propagate through the graph.
statement: Defines a derivation dependency graph G_D=(V,E_D) with Deps(A) giving direct premise sets, through which uncertainty can propagate.

anchor: But propagation depends on the inference method ... y=2x ... \sigma_y=2\sigma_x=0.2 ... a mathematical propagation rule. But now consider ... x is probably caused by y ... an abductive inference. Its uncertainty cannot be propagated using the same formula. PropagationFunction depends on InferenceMet
statement: Shows via a linear-uncertainty-propagation example (y=2x, σ_y=2σ_x) contrasted with an abductive inference that the propagation function itself depends on the inference method, not a single universal formula.

anchor: Deterministic derivation ... A_1\vdash Q ... the derivation itself does not introduce statistical uncertainty. However, the premises may still have epistemic uncertainty. Deterministic rule \not\Rightarrow uncertain premises. The rule may be certain while its inputs are not.
statement: Distinguishes rule certainty from premise certainty: a deterministic derivation rule does not itself add uncertainty, but its premises may still be epistemically uncertain — Deterministic rule ⇏ uncertain premises.

anchor: Statistical inference ... \hat\theta=10.2 with SE(\hat\theta)=0.4. The uncertainty belongs to the statistical inference. KnowledgeOS must preserve Estimate=10.2 and Uncertainty=0.4 rather than reducing the output to 10.2.
statement: Requires KnowledgeOS to preserve a statistical estimate together with its standard error (e.g. 10.2 ± 0.4) rather than collapsing to the point estimate alone.

anchor: Correlated evidence ... E_2=Copy(E_1), then Information(E_2\mid E_1)\approx0. Dependency structure must participate in uncertainty/support propagation.
statement: Restates that strongly correlated/copied evidence adds near-zero additional information, so dependency structure must participate in uncertainty/support propagation, not be treated as independent.

anchor: Unknown dependency ... a conservative policy might produce Support_{combined}\leq Support_{assuming independence}. But that inequality is policy-dependent, not a universal mathematical theorem. The kernel should preserve Dependency=Unknown. The assessment calculus decides what to do.
statement: Notes a conservative policy may cap combined support below the independence assumption when dependency is unknown, but this inequality is policy-dependent, not a universal theorem — the kernel only preserves Dependency=Unknown.

anchor: The most important statistical distinction ... P(A)=0.9 and P(B)=0.9 ... If independent P(A\land B)=0.81. If perfectly dependent P(A\land B)=0.9. Marginal confidence does not determine joint confidence. This is a major reason KnowledgeOS cannot use naive confidence multiplication.
statement: Uses two 0.9-confidence propositions to show joint confidence ranges from 0.81 (independent) to 0.9 (perfectly dependent) — marginal confidence does not determine joint confidence, ruling out naive confidence multiplication.

anchor: Statistical propagation needs a model ... Y=f(X_1,\ldots,X_n) ... Var(Y)\approx J\Sigma_XJ^T ... Covariance matters. This maps beautifully to our evidence-dependency model.
statement: Notes formal statistical uncertainty propagation Var(Y)≈JΣ_XJ^T requires the full covariance matrix, mapping naturally onto the evidence-dependency model — covariance matters, not just marginal uncertainties.

anchor: KnowledgeOS should therefore preserve dependency, not just scores ... A1 confidence = 0.9, A2 confidence = 0.9 ... instead A1, A2, Dependency(A1,A2) = Independent / Dependent / Unknown. Then a calculus can determine the appropriate combination. This is one of the strongest architectural consequences
statement: Argues KnowledgeOS must store per-pair Dependency status alongside confidence scores rather than bare scores alone, called one of the strongest architectural consequences of the theory.

anchor: Derived knowledge should retain its dependency graph ... A_3=f(A_1,A_2). Basis(A_3)=\{A_1,A_2\}. If A_1 is retracted, we do not automatically retract A_3. Instead Reassess(A_3). This follows directly from Step 9.
statement: Requires derived assertions retain their basis (Basis(A3)={A1,A2}), so retracting one premise triggers Reassess, not automatic retraction — following directly from Step 9's dependency-propagation invariant.

anchor: Support propagation ... S_3=PropagateSupport_\rho(S_1,S_2,R,D,C) ... S_3=\min(S_1,S_2) ... S_3=S_1\times S_2 ... S_3=f(S_1,S_2,D). There is no universal formula.
statement: Defines abstract support propagation S_3=PropagateSupport_ρ(S1,S2,R,D,C), showing min, product, and dependency-adjusted formulas as different rule-specific instances — no universal formula.

anchor: Uncertainty propagation ... U_3=PropagateUncertainty_\rho(U_1,U_2,R,D,C) ... The kernel stores uncertainty semantics; the calculus performs uncertainty propagation.
statement: Defines U_3=PropagateUncertainty_ρ(U1,U2,R,D,C) analogously to support propagation, with the architecture rule that the kernel stores uncertainty semantics while the calculus performs the actual propagation.

anchor: A useful distinction: epistemic versus aleatory uncertainty ... Aleatory uncertainty Intrinsic variability/randomness ... Epistemic uncertainty Uncertainty caused by lack of knowledge ... We don't know which version is deployed. KnowledgeOS primarily deals with epistemic uncertainty, but may also en
statement: Distinguishes aleatory uncertainty (intrinsic randomness, e.g. X~N(μ,σ²)) from epistemic uncertainty (lack of knowledge, e.g. unknown deployed version), noting KnowledgeOS primarily deals with the latter but should not collapse the two when both are relevant.

anchor: Example: infrastructure ... Backup configured ... Restore test succeeded ... Backup is operationally recoverable. A_1,A_2\Rightarrow A_3. But suppose A_2 is missing. Then A_1 alone may support Configured but not OperationallyRecoverable. Missing premise \Rightarrow Derived proposition remains unreso
statement: Worked backup-recoverability example showing that a missing premise (no restore test) leaves the derived proposition unresolved rather than falsely supported.

anchor: This gives us a concept of inference sufficiency ... Complete(R,\Gamma) meaning all required premises are available at the required epistemic level. Complete(R,\Gamma)=False \Rightarrow A_3 cannot be deductively derived. An LLM may still hypothesize A_3, but it must not label it as deterministic der
statement: Defines inference-sufficiency predicate Complete(R,Γ): if false, A3 cannot be deductively derived, though an LLM may hypothesize it as long as it is never mislabeled deterministic derivation.

anchor: Partial derivation ... Candidate(A_3) and MissingPremise(A_2). This directly generates a discrepancy \Delta_{missing premise}. Lord can then search for evidence for A_2. So inference becomes another mechanism for gap discovery. Inference \rightarrow MissingPremise \rightarrow Discrepancy \rightarrow
statement: Shows a missing premise generates a Candidate(A3)+MissingPremise(A2) state that becomes a discrepancy Lord can act on, establishing the feedback loop Inference→MissingPremise→Discrepancy→EvidenceAcquisition — inference as another gap-discovery mechanism, i.e. KnowledgeOS can infer what it needs to know in order to infer what it wants to know.

anchor: Uncertainty propagation through chains ... A_1\rightarrow A_2\rightarrow A_3\rightarrow A_4 ... For a probabilistic model P(A_4\mid A_1) ... For deterministic rules A_1\vdash A_2\vdash A_3\vdash A_4. For defeasible rules, an intermediate conclusion may be defeated later. InferenceDepth can affect ep
statement: Shows chained inference (A1→A2→A3→A4) behaves differently under probabilistic, deterministic, and defeasible rule regimes — inference depth affects reliability, but through no single universal formula.

anchor: LLM chains ... Document → LLM extraction → Assertion A1 → LLM interpretation → Assertion A2 → LLM synthesis → Assertion A3 ... We must preserve the entire chain: D\rightarrow A_1\rightarrow A_2\rightarrow A_3. A3 inherits dependency on the entire chain. This does not mean its uncertainty must be num
statement: Traces an LLM extraction→interpretation→synthesis chain (Document→A1→A2→A3), requiring the full lineage preserved even though numerical uncertainty need not be multiplied along the chain.

anchor: This distinction is essential ... Uncertainty propagation A mathematical transformation of uncertainty. Provenance propagation Preservation of the causal/derivational basis. KnowledgeOS must always do provenance propagation. It may do quantitative uncertainty propagation only when the chosen calculu
statement: Distinguishes universal Provenance propagation (always required) from calculus-dependent Numerical uncertainty propagation (only when the chosen calculus supports it) — called a major theoretical result.

anchor: Derived epistemic state ... \Sigma_D = F_\rho(\Sigma_1,\ldots,\Sigma_n,R,D,C) ... Acquisition=Derived and Method=R.Method. Acquisition = Derived, Method = Deduction, Rule = R-17 ... or Method = StatisticalInference, Model = M-04 ... or Acquisition = Generated, Method = LLMInterpretation.
statement: Defines the derived epistemic state Σ_D=F_ρ(Σ1,...,Σn,R,D,C) requiring an explicit Acquisition=Derived/Generated field and Method (Deduction/Rule, StatisticalInference/Model, LLMInterpretation) recorded per assertion.

anchor: Validity propagation ... Validity(A_2) \subseteq Validity(A_1) may be appropriate. But if another premise has shorter validity, A_2 may be constrained by the intersection Validity(A_2) \subseteq \bigcap_i Validity(A_i). Again, the exact semantics are policy-dependent.
statement: Defines validity propagation for derived assertions: Validity(A2)⊆Validity(A1) in the simple case, or the intersection over all premises when several bound it, with the exact semantics policy-dependent.

anchor: Temporal propagation ... A derived assertion ... should not silently become current in 2026. TemporalValidity must propagate through derivation.
statement: Requires temporal validity to propagate through derivation, so a derived assertion about a 2024-valid premise does not silently become current later.

anchor: Conflict propagation ... A_3=f(A_1) may therefore inherit a dependency on the contested premise. It need not automatically become contested, but KnowledgeOS should know DependsOnContested(A_3,A_1). Propagation of dependency \neq automatic propagation of status.
statement: Distinguishes dependency propagation from status propagation: a derived assertion depending on a contested premise is recorded as DependsOnContested, without automatically inheriting the Contested status itself — that remains a policy decision.

anchor: A formal dependency operator ... D(A) ... transitive dependencies are D^*(A) ... D^*(A) = \bigcup_{x\in D(A)}(\{x\}\cup D^*(x)). This gives us a computable dependency closure for finite acyclic derivation graphs.
statement: Defines the transitive dependency closure D*(A)=∪_{x∈D(A)}({x}∪D*(x)), computable for finite acyclic derivation graphs.

anchor: Cyclic inference ... A_1\rightarrow A_2 and A_2\rightarrow A_1. We have a cycle. KnowledgeOS should not blindly use recursive support amplification. Cycles require explicit fixpoint or cycle policy. ... Fixpoint semantics ... K^*=T(K^*) ... whether a fixpoint exists, is unique, and is computable dep
statement: Warns cyclic inference (A1→A2→A1) must never blindly amplify support, requiring an explicit fixpoint (K*=T(K*)) or cycle policy, with monotonicity (K1⊆K2⇒T(K1)⊆T(K2)) required for well-behaved iterative closure and explicit revision semantics needed when it fails.

anchor: Computational conclusion ... Can uncertainty and derivation be computed? Yes, when: the evidence graph is finite; inference rules are explicit; dependency relationships are represented; the selected calculus is computationally defined; uncertainty semantics are specified. But: There is no universal
statement: Concludes uncertainty/derivation computation is tractable under five conditions (finite graph, explicit rules, represented dependencies, computationally-defined calculus, specified uncertainty semantics), while there is no universal algorithm for arbitrary natural-language inference — Computable kernel operations must be distinguished from AI-assisted semantic interpretation.

anchor: KnowledgeOS computational contract ... Every computationally asserted result must declare its inference method and its derivation basis. Derived(A) \Rightarrow (Method(A),Premises(A),Rule/Model(A),Version(A)). If these are unavailable: Status(A)\neq DeterministicallyDerived.
statement: States the computational contract: every derived assertion must declare Method, Premises, Rule/Model, and Version — absent these, its status can never be DeterministicallyDerived.

anchor: The complete uncertainty model ... A=(P,E,\Sigma,\Omega,D,\Pi,Ctx,\tau) ... \Sigma=(Acquisition,Support,Uncertainty,Validity) ... \Omega=(Acceptance,Commitment,Contest) ... D=DependencyGraph.
statement: Consolidates the assertion model as A=(Proposition,Evidence,Σ,Ω,DependencyGraph,Provenance,Context,Time), integrating the epistemic (Σ) and governance (Ω) states with an explicit dependency graph.

anchor: The most important Step 11 principles ... U1 — Preserve uncertainty ... U2 — Method dependence ... U3 — Dependency dependence ... U4 — Provenance is universal ... U5 — Unknown dependency remains unknown ... U6 — Revision triggers reassessment ... U7 — Missing premises remain gaps ... U8 — Statistica
statement: States ten candidate invariants U1-U10: derived knowledge must not silently become certain; propagation depends on inference method; dependency affects aggregation; provenance is universally retained; unknown≠independent; premise revision triggers dependent reassessment; missing premises remain gaps (unresolved inference); statistical uncertainty is retained; LLM output ≠ deterministic derivation; derived chains must not create independent evidence merely through repetition.

anchor: Step 11 verdict ... THEORETICALLY RESOLVED AT THE FRAMEWORK LEVEL ... KnowledgeOS does not need one universal uncertainty formula. It needs a universal uncertainty contract. Origin + Method + Dependency + Provenance + UncertaintySemantics + Validity. The selected inference/assessment calculus then d
statement: Declares Step 11 theoretically resolved at the framework level with the major result that KnowledgeOS needs a universal uncertainty contract (Origin+Method+Dependency+Provenance+UncertaintySemantics+Validity), not a universal uncertainty formula.

anchor: Where we are after Step 11 ... Input \rightarrow Evidence \rightarrow Relations \rightarrow Assessment \rightarrow Acceptance \rightarrow KnowledgeState \rightarrow Discrepancy \rightarrow CandidateAction \rightarrow NewEvidence \rightarrow Inference \rightarrow DerivedKnowledge \rightarrow Uncertai
statement: Assembles the full pipeline from Input through Evidence/Relations/Assessment/Acceptance/KnowledgeState/Discrepancy/CandidateAction/NewEvidence/Inference/DerivedKnowledge/UncertaintyPropagation to RevisedKnowledgeState, with provenance preserved across the entire chain.

anchor: Step 12 — The next problem ... How does KnowledgeOS know that two propositions actually refer to the same thing, concept, entity, event, or state? ... "Nexus" "Nexus Repository" "Nexus3" "nexus3.dgverlag.de" "the artifact repository" "the old Nexus server" ... Step 12 — Identity, Entity Resolution,
statement: Poses Step 12: identity, entity resolution, and semantic equivalence across differently-named references to the same entity (six example Nexus aliases) and differently-worded but possibly equivalent propositions, called one of the most important remaining computational tests since duplicate/contradiction/dependency/aggregation/update reliability all depend on it.

lineage_claims.quote: Step 12 -- Identity, Entity Resolution, and Semantic Equivalence

anchor: If identity is wrong, everything downstream can be wrong. ... Nexus / Nexus Repository / Nexus3 / nexus3.dgverlag.de / the artifact repository / the old Nexus server ... Same name\neq Same entity ... Different name\neq Different entity. This becomes a fundamental KnowledgeOS principle.
statement: States the fundamental principle SameName≠SameEntity and DifferentName≠DifferentEntity, illustrated with six differently-named references possibly denoting the same Nexus system, and warns that identity errors propagate downstream through Comparison→Conflict→EvidenceAggregation→Inference→Discrepancy.

anchor: Three things must be separated ... Representation r ... Entity x ... Proposition P(x). Representation\neq Entity\neq Proposition
statement: Separates Representation (textual expression r), Entity (the referent x), and Proposition (a statement P(x) about that entity) as three distinct concepts.

anchor: DDD interpretation ... Identity — which domain object is this? Value — what does it represent? Context — where does this identity have meaning? Aggregate — what consistency boundary governs it? Reference — how do we locate it? ... KnowledgeEntity with a stable identity independent of how it happens
statement: Maps identity to five DDD concepts (Identity/Value/Context/Aggregate/Reference), introducing a KnowledgeEntity domain concept with stable identity independent of naming.

anchor: Canonical identity ... ID(x) ... EntityId: system:nexus:production ... multiple representations can resolve to it ... if sufficient evidence establishes Resolve(r_i)=x.
statement: Defines a canonical entity identifier ID(x) (e.g. system:nexus:production) to which multiple surface representations may resolve given sufficient evidence.

anchor: Resolution is not string matching ... Normalize("Nexus3")=Normalize("nexus3") and conclude identity. That is unsafe. Instead EntityResolution = f(Representation,Context,Evidence,IdentityRules). The output should itself have an epistemic status.
statement: Warns that string-normalization matching is unsafe for entity resolution, defining EntityResolution=f(Representation,Context,Evidence,IdentityRules) with an epistemic status on the output rather than a boolean.

anchor: Entity resolution is an inference ... Nexus3 is running on nexus3.dgverlag.de. We infer Entity("Nexus3")=Entity("nexus3.dgverlag.de"). But this is not necessarily directly observed. ... IdentityAssertion with evidence and provenance.
statement: Connects entity resolution to Step 10's inference machinery: identity claims are themselves inferences, not direct observations, and must be represented as an IdentityAssertion carrying evidence and provenance.

anchor: Identity assertion ... I_A=(r,x,S,Ctx,\Pi,\tau) ... "Nexus3" \equiv system:nexus:production. But KnowledgeOS should know why it believes that.
statement: Defines IdentityAssertion I_A=(representation,entity,Support,Context,Provenance,Validity) so KnowledgeOS always records why an identity claim is believed.

anchor: Identity is contextual ... Nexus means the Nexus product in one context ... the production deployment in another context. Meaning(Nexus,C_1)\neq Meaning(Nexus,C_2). Identity is interpreted within context. We should never create a universal global identity merely from a name.
statement: States identity is interpreted within context (Meaning(Nexus,C1)≠Meaning(Nexus,C2)) — a universal global identity must never be created merely from a name.

anchor:
Product versus instance ... NexusProduct versus NexusInstance_{Production} ... Software
eq Deployment
eq Container
eq Host
eq Service
eq Endpoint. A DDD model must preserve these distinctions.
statement: Distinguishes Product from Instance and six further layered concepts (Software/Deployment/Container/Host/Service/Endpoint) that a DDD model must preserve separately.

anchor: Entity identity can be hierarchical ... x_{product}, x_{deployment}, x_{host} ... DeploymentOf(x_{deployment},x_{product}) RunsOn(x_{deployment},x_{host}) ExposedAt(x_{deployment},endpoint). Thus identity is not just a flat lookup. It is a semantic graph. ... Entity graph G_X=(\mathcal X,\mathcal R_
statement: Defines a hierarchical Entity graph G_X=(X,R_X) with typed relations (DeploymentOf, RunsOn, ExposedAt) linking product/deployment/host/endpoint layers, arguing identity is a semantic graph, not a flat lookup.

anchor: Now semantic equivalence ... Version(Nexus)=3.69 and Nexus is running release 3.69 ... may be semantically equivalent. But Nexus was version 3.69 in 2024 is not equivalent to P_1 if P_1 is intended to describe the current state. ... Define semantic equivalence P_1\equiv_C P_2 ... The context subscri
statement: Defines context-relative semantic equivalence P1≡_C P2, warning that without the context subscript equivalence becomes dangerously absolute, illustrated by a temporally-scoped proposition that is not equivalent to a current-state one.
